-The classical way to play this variation is to castle kingside, then launch the f-pawn forward to pressure Black's light squares and start a same-side kingside attack. While this line might be playable, it has been shown that black could equalise without facing major problems from white. The modern improvement to this variant is to first play Qf3-Qg3, making the queen an active contributor in the attack.
-Modern systems planning to castle queenside are promising. White intends to attack Black's kingside even more aggressively, and she has options of dropping explosive piece sacrifices on e6. An example line: 6...e6 7. Bb3 b5 8. Be3!? Be7 9. Qf3 Qc7 10. g4 b4 11. Nce2, where Black must play very accurately to survive.
-An important alternative is the Velimirović attack, developed by Serbian grandmaster Dragoljub Velimirović, where White plays Bb3, Be3, Qe2, O-O-O and prepares a kingside attack with Rg1 and g2-g4. This is another system where Black must be precise to survive.
-7. a4 is a reputable sideline, stopping ...b7-b5 and aiming to develop with Be3 and Qe2 just like in the Velimirović attack, but usually castles kingside and pushes f2-f4.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2
column3: Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6. Be2\n6. Be2 is not played as often in response to black pushing 5. ...a6 as is 6. Bg5 or 6. Be3, but it is a solid move. White's bishop at e2 can keep an eye on g4 while allowing for a king side castle.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3
column3:
6. Be3 is the English attack. White has an idea to castle long and storm Black's kingside with their pawns.
6...e5 is the main line. This drives off White's knight to b3, but weakens d5 which White will try to use as an outpost.
6...Ng4 is the Anti-English. Black tries to avert White's plans of a kingside attack by trading off White's important dark square bishop. Whereas in the Yugoslav attack against the Dragon Sicilian, 6. Be3 Ng4?? is a mistake on account of 7. Bb5+! Nc6 8. Nxc6 bxc6 9. Bxc6+ Bd7 10. Bxa8, the difference in the Najdorf is that Black has played ...a6, so White does not have the resource Bb5+, therefore ...Ng4 is safe.
6...e6 builds a "small centre" and transposes into a Scheveningen Scillian. This is move order ju-jitsu to play the Scheveningen without facing the Keres attack, 5...e6 6. g4!. In that line, Black cannot play 6...e5 on account of the Bb5+ resource. However, in the move order 5...a6 6. Be3 e6, Black's a6 pawn prevents Bb5+, so 7. g4!? can be met with ...e5!, a discovered attack on g4 and threatening ...exd4 with a fork.
6. Be3 is the most popular way for White to combat the Najdorf. It has been played since the 1950s, but 6. Bg5 was more typical until the 1980s, when 6. Be3 was popularised by English grandmasters like Tony Miles, John Nunn and Nigel Short.
The approach--long castle and pawn storm--had been the standard approach against the Dragon Sicilian, the Yugoslav attack, since at least the 1930s.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5
column3: Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5\nBlack must react in order to avoid doubled pawns on the f file. The most popular and almost only available option is 6...e6.\n6...Nbd7 is also playable.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Rg1
column3: The Freak Attack is a very recent and upcoming response to the Najdorf. White's idea is to prepare a quick g2-g4, in style of the Keres Attack, combined with h4 and f4 causing problems to black's kingside. It also allows the bishop to develop to h3 in the future. Even though Rg1 looks absurd at first glance, it is a totally sound option according to the strongest engines. It is also a great surprise weapon - Theory is still developing on it and engine lines are still not sure how to proceed.\nOf course, like every move, it is not the best choice either. White has forfeited kingside castling, so black can concentrate on the center and the queenside instead. White also leaves a massive hole on f3 -- While covered for now by the knight and the queen, black can later make use of the backward f2 pawn. And finally, black can prevent white's apparent plan with an immediate h5, which also has a massive winrate so far.\nThe antidote to the entire variation is considered to be ...e5 Nb3 Be6 g4 d5!. Black strikes back in the center and a series of trades occur leaving both sides with a minimal amount of pieces to proceed into the game, and white's kingside assault plan is halted before it even starts.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Bc4
column3: White enters the Sozin Attack, a direct and aggressive system named after Russian master Veniamin Sozin. By placing the bishop on c4, White eyes the vulnerable f7 square and sets the stage for a fast kingside assault. This move fits perfectly against the Scheveningen setup, where Black’s e6 pawn can make the light squares around the king more tender.\nTypical ideas for White include Qe2, Bb3, 0–0, and f4–f5, often leading to sharp play. In response, Black must tread carefully—failing to play ...Be7 and ...0–0 promptly can invite devastating attacks. The Sozin is a favorite of players seeking initiative and imbalances, and was famously wielded by Bobby Fischer with great success.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 g4
column3:
White's 6. g4 begins the Keres Attack, a sharp and important line in the Scheveningen Variation.
Black's previous move, 5...e6, boxes in his light squared bishop and relinquishes control over the g4 square. Now, White advances his g pawn with the idea of following with 7. g5, pushing black's f knight back and winning more space on the kingside. Note that against the Sicilian, White often opens up a kingside pawn storm, such as in the English Attack, and 6. g4 furthers that goal well.
Black's most common response, therefore, is 6...h6, preventing the g pawn from advancing. Other responses, such as 6...Nc6, do not discourage the g pawn push, and are therefore usually followed by 7. g5 Nd7. Now black's kingside knight has been pushed back into a much more passive position and white's pawns are dangerously close to black's kingside, if black chooses to castle there. After 6...h6 Black should certainly not proceed to castle kingside quickly against this line.
Attempting to counterattack with 6...e5 is easily met by 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.Bxd7+ Qxd7 9.Nb3. White has traded off light squared bishops, and is preparing to set up the standard English Attack. Note that this is one reason that many Scheveningen players use a Najdorf move order first and transpose to the Scheveningen. In this case, the presence of the a6 pawn discourages Bb5+, and lines here in which white plays g4 are referred to as the Perenyi Attack rather than the Keres Attack.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be2
column3: This variation is a variation of the Sicilian tradition of the dragon. White wants to make a great defence in kingside.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3
column3:
White develops their bishop. This prepares to castle queenside and usually leads to the Yugoslav attack.
6...Bg7 is the most logical and main line continuation, developing the bishop as prepared by ...g6 and preparing to castle.
6...Nc6 is an alternative. This is really a waiting move where Black delays committing their bishop. 7. f3 h5 is the Hungarian variation, and Black has the idea of meeting 8. Qd2 with 8...Nxd4 9. Bxd4 Bh6! 10. Be3 Bxe3 11. Qxe3, trading off the minor pieces and so easing the discomfort of being down on space.
If Black is tempted to play 6...Ng4??, hoping to chop off White's dark-squared Bishop and leave their bishop unopposed, they should be warned that this a beginner's mistake which loses horribly to 7. Bb5+.
7...Nd7 8. Qxg4 wins the knight.
7...Bd7 8. Qxg4 also wins the knight, since the Bishop on d7 is pinned.
7...Nc6 8. Nxc6 bxc6 9. Bxc6+, forking the king and rook and winning the exchange and a pawn.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 f4
column3:
This move has a few ideas connoted to it. The primary idea is to push e5, since this pawn idea gains central influence and is now prepared by f4. White can also look to put the knight back onto f3 and play the position like a Grand Prix attack, with future ideas of swinging the white queen onto the kingside through the e1-h4 diagonal. Against some sidelines, white can also consider castling long!
The natural looking 6...Bg7 is actually theoretically inaccurate. This runs into White's primary idea of the Levenfish, to push e5. White does this immediately with 7. e5 and then can claim a slight, nagging edge in the upcoming variations because of the advanced e-pawn.
White should seek active play with Bb5+ and Qe2 to support the pawn before deciding which way to castle, both leading to viable positions
The best move since it immediately covers the threat of e5. This idea effectively killed the Levenfish variation pre-2000. Black develops the queenside knight. Here, White has traditionally gone for the line 7. Nxc6!? bxc6 8. e5 which is somewhat favourable for black upon 8...Nd7! 9. exd6 exd6 leading to an interesting pawn structure. A sounder alternative several high profile games have included is the idea of 7. Nf3!? swinging the knight back to the kingside and looking to play a slower game on the kingside.
6...Nbd7 is traditionally met by 7. Nf3, although in recent times engines have preferred queen developments such as 7. Qe2, the choice of Grandmaster Gevorg Harutjunyan.
6...a6 aims to stop a piece landing on b5 and constructs a sort of Dragondorf setup. Here White can choose between 7. e5 and 7. Nf3.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 Bc4
column3: 6.Bc4 begins the Sozin attack on the classical Sicilian. Black may choose to reply with e6, which is a position easily reached through transposition from the Scheveningen variation as well (6.Bc4,Nc3). However, from the Scheveningen variation white tends to pick other attacks which are more suited to the position, such as the English Attack or the Keres Attack. The Sozin attack is often considered less common and less ambitious than the Richter-Rauzer Attack.\nBlack could also choose to reply with g6 transposing to a form of the Dragon variation, but this leads to the "Magnus Smith trap," with a lot of trouble for black (see a YouTube analysis here).\nIf black does play e6, both players typically develop bishops with white playing Be3 and black responding with Be7. In this position if white castles king side it is called the Fisher-Sozin attack. If white instead moves Qe2 and eventually castles queenside it is called the Velimirovic variation.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 Bg5
column3:
Traditionally, in the Classical Sicilian, Black aims for ...e5 or ...g6. The Richter-Rauser (also spelt Richter-Rauzer) is a way for white to combat both of these ideas. It does not completely stop either of the ideas, but it does make them less desirable. ...g6 would weaken the defense of the Black knight on f6.
6...e5 in this position would be considered winning for White and detrimental to the Black position, as after White captures the knight with 7. Bxf6, Black has to choose between capturing back with the g-pawn, or with the Queen:
Option 1: Taking back with 7...gxf6 is the better of the two options according to engine analysis, although it comes with White gaining an outpost for its knight after 8. Nf5. Black could attempt to dislodge the knight with 9...d5, but this can be met with 10. Qxd5. Exchanging Queens immediately is not good for Black, as after 10...Qxd5 11. Nxd5, White is threatening to fork the Black King and Rook with Nc7+. Black is forced to exchange its Light-Squared Bishop with 11...Bxf5 12. exf5. Black then castles with 12...O-O-O, and White wins a pawn.
Option 2: Taking back on f6 with the Black Queen (7...Qxf6) is the worst of the two options and gives White double the advantage. White moves his knight with 8. Ndb5 threaten Nc7+, forking the King and Rook. Defending with the Queen isn't feasible, as White can simply place his other knight on d5 with a nice outpost, and c7 is weak again. If White attempts to defend with the King, with either 8...Kd8 or 8...Kd7, White can play 9. Nc7!!, sacrificing the knight, because if the Black King captures (9...Kxc7??) White can play 10. Nd5! forking the Black King and Queen.
However, it must be kept in mind this opening is fairly theoretical, and there are several playing options for both sides that can lead to a variety of positions.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nb5 d6 c4
column3: White sets up the Maroczy bind structure to control d5. Between their c and e pawns, and having induced Black to play d6 and restrict their own dark square bishop, they hope to keep Black's position cramped, hampering their development, and that this will make up for the loss of tempo White incurred in moving their knight multiple times in the opening.\nIf 6...a6 straight away, Black kicks White's knight and they are forced to move it again: usually to c3.\nBlack usually plays 6...Nf6 first, threatening Nxe4 with the idea of inducing 7. N1c3, followed by 7...a6 to kick the knight to 8. Na3 where it is on the rim and therefore grim, but from where it overprotect the c4 pawn and doesn't obstruct the White queen's support of d5.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5
column3: Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 6.Ndb5\nThe White knight's threat of check on d6 is a bit awkward: ...Ke7 would be unpleasant so Black would have to surrender his bishop with ...Bxd6, only to have a queen arrive on d6 and single-handedly cramp the whole Black position. She would need to go, too: ...Qe7 Qxe7 Kxe7/Nxe7, and suddenly Black's dodgy d-pawn and slow development are significant factors in the much simplified position. Far better to keep the knight out of d6 for now and then vanquish it to a3 in a move's time with 6...d6.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nc3 e6 g4 Bg6 Nge2
column3: White threatens Nf4 and h4, so Black must react. Black usually counters in the centre with 6... c5.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5 cxd5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 Bg5
column3: With this move, White immediately threatens the d5 pawn. Here, Black can simply capture the c pawn with 6...dxc4, or defend the d pawn with 6...e6 or even the strange-looking but perfectly sound 6...Be6, when Black usually fianchettos the dark-squared bishop.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5 cxd5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3
column3: 6. Nf3 is the main line for white, and black has a number of alternatives here. The more solid 6... e6, fianchettoing the bishop with 6... g6, or the main line, 6... Bg4, which leads to somewhat crazy positions that black can safely navigate if they know what they're doing.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4
column3: Black needs to defend the bishop, and h6 is almost universal, although the probably inferior h5 and Nd7 have been attempted.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng5 Bg6 N1f3
column3: White plays Nf3 and is about to counterattack. However, black rarely understands and notices it. There are a few popular replies to this, but black usually responds with h6, trying to kick out the knight, who's been a pain in the neck for a while.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng5 h6 Nxf7
column3:
White grabs the f7 pawn with 6. Nxf7?, entering the dubious but incredibly scary Alien Gambit, popularized by YouTuber Witty Alien! This gambit is losing for White and can be punished with careful play; as such, it is mostly used in Bullet and Blitz.
The purpose of this move is to ruin Black's kingside structure by creating several light-squared holes in Black's kingside; force the Black king to recapture, giving up castling rights; and take Black out of their comfort zone, since most Caro-Kann players are mostly used to slow, positional grinds rather than tactical skirmishes. The Alien Gambit is an attack on Black's weak light squares on the kingside. When the knight grabs the f7 pawn, Black has several light-squared holes on e6 and g6 which can quickly be pounced on by White's pieces, often leading to checkmate for White on these very squares.
Black has two approaches to send the aliens back to their desolate sector of the cosmos: one is to attack White's weak dark squares with c5, Nc6, and so on; another is to defend the light squares with Be6, develop the knight with Nbd7, and counterattack on the light squares. Both of these approaches can even be combined seamlessly, leading to the aliens' demise.
Black must respect White's attack on the light squares. After Nxf7? Kxf7 Nf3 Bg4?? (which is the most common response), White can play Ne5! and win the knight back with a monstrous attack on the light squares to follow.

column1: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4 Kf1
column3:
6...Nh6: Silberschmidt Defence
6...Nc6: Viennese Variation
6...f3: Cochrane Gambit
6...Nf6: Santa Maria Defence

column1: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 O-O gxf3 Qxf3
column3: White recaptures with their queen and prepares to start a big attack as compensation for the lost knight. White attacks the f4 pawn and this is really a major threat; for example, 6...Nc6?, the so-called Holloway Defence, runs into trouble after 7. Qxf4! Qe7 (if 7...Nh6??, 8. Bxf7+! Ke7 9. Qf6# ends the game) 8. Bxf7+! Kd8 9. Nc3! (threatening Nd5). Black has two main options:\n6...Qf6, the Sarratt Defence, is almost always played, defending the attacked f4 pawn while adding another defender to the weak f7 square and challenging White to prove sufficient compensation for the material loss.\n6...Qe7, the From's Defence, has an interesting idea. If White gets greedy and captures the seemingly free f4 pawn, 7...Qc5+! picks up the bishop on c4.

column1: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4 g4 Ne5 Nf6 Bc4
column3: Black has to do something about the attack by the White bishop and knight on f7. The bishop's diagonal must be blocked at the cost of a pawn with 6...d5.

column1: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nxe4 Qh5 Nd6 Bb3 Nc6 Nb5
column3:
With his last move, 6. Nb5, White has launched a very dangerous attack against Black's Nd6, the key piece of the defence, which is immobilized (6...Nxb5?? 7. Qxf7#). White now menaces the obvious 7. Nxd6+, leading to a forced mate (7...cxd6?? 8. Qxf7#; 7...Ke7 8.Nf5+ Kf6 9. Qxf7+ Kg5 10. Nh3+ Kg4 11. f3#).
The only solution for Black is to defend f7 with another piece, and the only one available is the Queen. However, after 6...Qe7? or 6...Qf6?, White may play 7. Nxc7+ followed by 8. Nxa8, gaining the exchange.
This material loss is unavoidable, but, before it happens, Black has the opportunity to improve his position with some intermediate moves, advancing the pawns to block White Queen's attack lines. On the other hand, White can repropose the mate threat, moving his Queen to different offensive positions. Therefore, the game continues:
6...g6 7. Qf3 f5 8. Qd5
At this point, Black can no more defer the protection of f7 with his Queen, and therefore he is forced to allow the Knight fork on c7:
8...Qe7 (or 8...Qf6) 9. Nxc7+ Kd8 10. Nxa8
In order to sacrifice only the exchange, and not the whole Rook, Black then plays
10...b6,
preparing Bb7.
The final result of this sharp sequence is the Frankenstein-Dracula Variation.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 f5 Bc4 fxe4 Nxe5 Qg5 Nf7 Qxg2 Rf1
column3: White moves their rook to safety. Black will now start an attack with 6...d5!. White will have to navigate safely. 6...Nf6 and 6...Nc6 are also playable but are risky. Any other move and the attack runs out of fuel.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 b5 Bb3 Na5 Bxf7
column3: 6. Bxf7+!\nAs we can see here, White played the unexpected move 6. Bxf7+!, sacrificing the Bishop to abuse the position of Black after 6...Kxf7 7. Nxe5 7...Kf6 8.Qh5 8...c6 9.Qf7+! & White has a huge advantage. This is known as the Nightingale Gambit. This is by far the most aggressive & sharp move after 5...Na5.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O b5 Bb3
column3: The move ...b5 is seen at some point in most variations of the main line Ruy Lopez, so Black has a few transpositional possibilities here: 6...d6 or 6...Be7 will probably end up in the standard Closed Variation (5...Be7 6. Re1 b5) and 6...Nxe4 almost certainly leads back to the Open Variation.\nBasically, replacing ...Be7 with ...b5 means that Black has retained the option of setting up bishops at b7 and c5. The two independent moves, therefore, are the Arkhangelsk 6...Bb7 and the Møller 6...Bc5. They may transpose into each other.\nIt's always to Black's advantage to have something to play against the Lopez other than the old main lines, which is why these two sound, aggressive variations, along with 5...Bc5, have experienced a major revival of late.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Bxc6
column3:
By playing 4. Ba4 instead of 4. Bxc6, only to play 6. Bxc6, White has lost a tempo by moving their bishop twice. However, by waiting until Black has committed to ...Nf6, White prevents ...f6 to defend the e5 pawn (as in the Exchange variation, 4. Bxc6 dxc6 5. O-O f6). By also waiting until after ...Be7, White ensures that Black loses the tempo back if they defend the pawn with ...Bd6 (as in the Delayed exchange or Bayreuth variation, 4. Ba4 Nf6 5. Bxc6 dxc6 6. d3 Bd6).
After 6...dxc6 White can't win the e5 pawn straight because their e4 pawn is still hanging. First White defends their pawn with 7. d3 or 7. Re1. Black can defend e5 but give up their counterattack with ...Nd7, or pin White's knight to their queen with ...Bg4.
7. Qe2 also defends e4, but White still can't win the e5 pawn because of the tactic ...Qd4!.
7. Qe1 is an interesting alternative: this does defends against ...Nxe4 but White will still need to play ...d6 if they hope to win the e5 pawn due to the above-mentioned ...Qd4! tactic. Qe1 prevents Bg4 from pinning the knight. 7...Qg6 is probably best. 7...Bd6?! leads to 8. d4! exd4? 9. e5!. If 8...Qe7 9.dxe5! Bxe5 10. Nxe5 Qxe5 11. Qc3 Ng4 12. Qxe5+ Nxe5 13. f4! Ng6 14 .f5! (14. Be3 is also good) Ne5 15. Bf4 and White stands much better because of his better pawn structure.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Qe2
column3: The plan is to hold e4 with the queen and move the rook to d1 in preparation for d2-d4, and again this has the drawback of putting the queen on the file most likely to be opened by Black.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1
column3:
Now the White's own e-pawn is defended, the threat Bxc6 & Nxe5 winning e5 becomes a serious problem for Black.
The main move, 6...b5, permanently cuts out any of that nonsense. Black usually follows with castling and playing ...d6, freeing their c6 knight from having to guard e5 and allowing their bishop to develop.
There's also 6...d6, the Averbakh variation. It looks like Black has just forgotten which order to play the moves in. In this line White can play 7. c3 before their bishop is kicked, so when ...b5 eventually comes the bishop can retreat to c2 in one move. White normally wants their bishop on c2, and this way they have saved a tempo compared to 6...b5 7. Bb3 followed by c3 and Bc2 later.
The advantage for Black is that after 7.c3 Black has time to play ...Bg4 before White has gotten in h3. Whenever a bishop appears on g4 in the Closed Ruy Lopez, White is going to have to play d3 and bring the queen's knight across to the kingside to drive the bishop away before considering d4. On the other other hand, Magnus Carlsen voluntarily plays d3 instead of d4 even without a bishop on g4, so the current verdict seems to be that 6...d6 loses a tempo for no reason.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4
column3:
White is threatening to win back material by capturing Black's e-pawn. More importantly, they threaten to create dangerous attacks on the e-file while Black is still uncastled.
Black needs to complete their development, and if possible reinforce the crusading knight on e4. The immediate 6...d5? would leave the c6-knight pinned, allowing the powerful 7. Nxe5!. To get to grips with the situation, Black needs 6...b5 to prepare ...d5 by chasing the bishop away.
If Black is unconcerned with opening the e-file, they can accept an extra pawn with 6...exd4?!, the chaotic Riga variation, which leads to a wonderful mess.
6...Be7!? is a semi-useful move. After 7. Re1 this leads to a big liquidation of the centre: 7...b5 8. Rxe4 d5 9. Nxe5 Nxe5 10. Rxe5 bxa4⩲ and Black can't castle without dropping the e7 bishop.
Unlike in the Berlin defence, 6...Nd6? does not come with tempo on White's bishop and so does not work.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 Re1
column3: A minor sideline. Black's best move is 6...Nc5, and White can't preserve the bishop pair.\nThis leads to 7. Bxc6 dxc6 8. d4 Ne6 9. Nxe5 Be7 10. Be3 0-0 11. c4 and either 11...Bf6 or 11...Bd6, with an equal position.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Bxc6 dxc6 O-O Bg4 h3
column3: This move looks natural, forcing Black's hand, but there is a surprising option for Black! 6...h5 is a surprising move that forces White's hand instead.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bb6 b5 Na5 Nxe5
column3: White takes the undefended pawn on e5 while also defending their attacked bishop and threatening Nxf7, which would win Black's rook to a fork. It is true Black could trade with 6...Nxc4, but after the recapture 7. Nxc4, White is a clean pawn up. So Black has two real options: 6...Nh6, the Lange Variation, defending f7, and 6...Qg5, the Hirschbach Variation, going on a counterattack instead.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4
column3:
White takes the whole center, attacking the pawn on e5 aggressively. Black can choose from four options:
6...exd4 is usually played.
6...d6 is the most solid move.
6...b5 is interesting.
6...Nf6 is a mistake.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 b4
column3: White sacrifices the d4 pawn for quick development and an open d file. White also attacks the Black bishop on c5, forcing it to move. Black can play either 6...Bb6 or 6...Be7.\nIn contrast to the Evans gambit, White doesn't sacrifice the b pawn. Because of this White has the threat of b5, forcing the knight to move to a5 or e7.\nThe Dubov gambit is named after the Russian GM Daniil Dubov, who used it to great success against Russian GM Sergey Karjakin in 2020 at the Russian Championship in Moscow. Before GM Daniil Dubov popularised 6. b4, it was used very rarely in high level chess except for a 9 year old Dutch NM that used it to defeat Anish Giri in 2009 and Levon Aronian in 2008 but lost to GM Gukesh in 2009. Recently, the Dubov gambit has been used in online games by very strong players including GM Hikaru Nakamura, former world chess champion Ding Liren and GM Daniil Dubov himself.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4
column3: White plays the natural recapture. Now the bishop will have to move to b4 or b6; in most cases, Black plays 6...Bb4+.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Bc5 e5
column3:
The Max Lange Attack can arise from several different opening lines, including the Two Knights Defense, Petroff's Defense, Scotch Gambit, Bishop's Opening, Center Game, and Giuoco Piano. Two of the most commonly seen move orders are 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 (the Two Knights Defense) 4.d4 exd4 5.0-0 Bc5 6.e5, and 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 (the Scotch Gambit) Bc5 5.0-0 Nf6 6.e5.
After 6.e5, Black has two main replies. Black's 6...Ng4 is playable, but rarely seen. More common is 6...d5, when the main line continues 7.exf6 dxc4 8.Re1+ Be6 9.Ng5 Qd5 (9...Qxf6?? 10.Nxe6 fxe6 11.Qh5+ followed by 12.Qxc5 is a notorious trap) 10.Nc3 Qf5 (10...dxc3?? 11.Qxd5 wins, since 11...Bxd5 is illegal) 11.Nce4 0-0-0 with complex play. Another line for White to try, a critical response, is after 6...d5, White plays 7.Bb5 with strong ideas for both sides, usually resulting in a slight edge for White.
An alternative for White is 8.fxg7 Rg8 9.Bg5, analysed by Lev Gutman and Stefan Bücker in Kaissiber, which they consider to be good for White. Black's usual response is 9...Be7 10.Bxe7 Kxe7.
When contributing to this Wikibook, please follow the conventions for organization.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Nxe4 Nc3
column3:
An unsound but interesting gambit played by White, never seen at a grandmaster level. It can arise from several openings, although most commonly, the Italian Game and Scotch Gambit.
White invites Black to break open the center by capturing the knight with either the pawn or knight. Willing to lose material, a strong initiative is gained as White gets fast development and weakens Black's king. The gambit aims to take full advantage of the opponent's main weakness: the open e-file with Black's uncastled king and knight. If Black decides to accept the gambit with 6...dxc3, it is critical that they know the correct refuting moves.
Black may answer with:
6...dxc3 accepting the gambit. Objectively, the best move to retain Black's advantage.
6...Nxc3 declining the gambit while keeping some advantage.
6...Nd6 declining the gambit.
6...d5 declining the gambit.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Nxe4 Re1
column3: White pins the greedy knight on e4. As f5 would be too slow and Qe7 is still a major piece pin, d5! is the only sensible followup.\nd5 is only temporary, however, as Bxd5! followed by Nc3! taking advantage of both pins on the heavy pieces equalizes. An immediate Nc3 is an option as well, though less common.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 b5 Bf1
column3:
6. Bf1! is a surprising move that un-develops the Bishop, but by guarding the g2 pawn with the bishop the threat of ...Qxd5 is nullified.
Now if 6...Qxd5?!, White can calmly answer 7. Nc3 with tempo, and once Black's queen is driven from the a8-h1 diagonal, e.g. after 7...Qc5, White can then snap up the pawn after all, 8. Bxb5!, and Black has no threats.
Though 6...Qxd5 may be off the table, Black's knight is still en prise and this must be resolved.
Black may consider moving the knight instead. 6...Nd4 is the main move. The knight guards b5 and pressures important squares in White's position. White is best to shoo it away immediately, leading to a trade of knights: 7. c3 Nxd5 8. cxd4 Qxg5 9. Bxb5+ Kd8 ⩲. White wins back the pawn and has a small edge. This is a transposition into the Fritz variation, where ...Nd4 is played on turn 5.
Ulvestad's original analysis suggested 6...h6?!, a counterattack on White's knight that recognised that Black was better after either 7. Nf3? or 7. dxc6?. However, in 1963 it was discovered that White can play 7. Nxf7! anyway, the Kurkin gambit, and after 7...Kxf7 8. dxc6 has run away with the pawns.
Why not simply take the pawn back with the knight? 6...Nxd5, as played in Carlsen-Gukesh, 2024, is good and has become more popular in recent years.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Na5 d3
column3: An attempt to fully hang onto the pawn. This variation does not inspire, giving up a good bishop for the currently out of play knight is not something many players would choose. Therefore this variation is seldom played.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Nxd5 d4
column3: A strong move which enables White to gain a theoretical edge while avoiding getting into the complexities of the Fried Liver Attack.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxf7
column3: 6. Nxf7! is an aggressive Knight sacrifice. With no sensible way to decline, Black's King becomes exposed while White gains momentum in development.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nxc6 bxc6 e5
column3:
6. e5
Black’s knight is attacked, so what options do they have?
It’s natural to retreat with 6...Nd5 and 6...Ne4. These moves aren’t losing per se, but Black can do better.
And that’s with 6...Qe7.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Qb6 a3
column3:
By playing 6. a3 White eliminates any possibility of a b4 intrusion. White is also preparing to assert themselves on the queenside via b2-b4. Furthermore, b2-b4 frees the c1 bishop from minding the b2 pawn.
Black has three main options in this position.
6...c4 is the main line. Black relieves the pressure in the centre and prevents White from playing b4.
6...Nh6 is the Lputian variation. Black tries to route the kingside knight to f5 without obstructing the dark-squared bishop's view of c5. Taking the knight with 7. Bxh6? would be unwise.
6...Bd7 is a quieter variation. Bd7 is going to be a useful move in nearly all advance French positions. Black is postponing the development of the kingside knight for now.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Qb6 Bd3
column3: White develops the light-squared bishop to d3. While White appears to have lost a pawn, 6...cxd4 7. cxd4 Nxd4? 8. Nxd4 Qxd4?? 9. Bb5+! would win Black's queen to a discovered attack. So Black must guard against Bb5 with check. Black can play 6...cxd4 7. cxd4 Bd7!, blocking the king from the Bb5+ and thus threatening to win the d4-pawn; alternatively, most played nowadays is 6...Bd7 immediately.\nAfter the variation of 6...Bd7, White could release the tension with 7. dxc5 Bxc5 8. O-O, where Black has to be careful; 8...Ne7?? allows 9. b4 to trap Black's bishop. Alternatively, after 7. O-O cxd4, White can continue to play the position in gambit style in one of three ways: A, the main line with 8. cxd4 Nxd4 9. Nxd4 Qxd4; B, with 8. cxd4 Nxd4 9. Nbd2, looking to keep a strong knight on f3; or C, in similar fashion to the Göring gambit with 7. O-O cxd4 8. Re1! dxc3 9. Nxc3. All three of these options are incredibly dangerous for Black, as White gets easy development and a massive attack.\nAfter the alternative of 6...cxd4 7. cxd4 Bd7!, White can transpose into options A or B described earlier with 8. O-O!, or chicken out of the gambit lines with 8. Be2, allowing the queen to defend the d4 pawn but getting a much less ambitious position.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 dxe4 f3
column3: White offers Black an exchange of pawns. Instead of accepting the gambit with 6...exf3 and allowing White to develop, Black should strike back with 6...c5, giving White the option to achieve tripled pawns on the c-file.\n6...b6, 6...Bd7, 6...e5 are also playable.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Ba5 b4
column3: This is by far White's best option. Black must now respond accurately.\n6...cxb4? is sub-optimal. It seems that Black hopes to make use of a potential discovered attack after pushing their pawn, but this opportunity won't present itself after 7. Nb5! Nc6 8. axb4 Bxb4+ 9. c3 ± as seen in Topalov - Ermenkov, Elenite 1994. White got to trade off the dark-squared bishops and place their knight on d6, where it can't be contested by pawns.\nInstead, 6...cxd4 should be played, exchanging the c-pawn for White's central pawn and attacking the knight on c3. This is known as the Armenian line, named after its use by Armenian grandmasters Rafael Vaganian and Smbat Lputian.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3 bxc3
column3:
This is the main line of the Winawer variation of the French defence. The Winawer is a sharp and tactical variation of the French. White usually attempts to take the undefended g-pawn with Qg4.
Black's best move is 6...Ne7, developing the knight such that it defends g8 and can possibly reroute to f5, where it pressures White's centre.
6...Qc7, the Classical variation, backs the c-pawn and develops the queen to a good square.
6...Qa5 enters the Portisch-Hook variation where Black tries to provoke some more queenside weaknesses early on.
6...Nc6 is the rarest of the variations. Black allows 7. Qg4 and has to defend their queenside with 7...g6, leading to some very weak dark squares around their kingside.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e5 Nfd7 Bxe7
column3: Recapturing with the king would be unnecessarily dangerous, so 6...Qxe7 is the only real response.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 Bd3 c5 c3
column3: White reinforces their pawn chain.\n6...Nc6 increases the pressure on d4, and Black can also add an attacker with ...Qb6. White can choose to defend it with 7. Ne2, meeting 7...Qb6 with 8. Nf3, or gambit it with 7. Ngf3.\n6...b6, the Botvinnik variation, prepares to trade off Black's bad bishop for White's good one.

column1: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 d6 c4 Nb6 exd6 cxd6 Nc3
column3: Black would very much like to put pressure on the d-pawn with ...Nc6 and ...Bg7. Playing 6...Nc6 now however runs into d4-d5, maybe even on the next move, and the knight will find itself kicked around the board. So Black is in most games patient, and plays 6...g6 to prepare 7...Bg7.

column1: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 d6 c4 Nb6 f4 dxe5 fxe5
column3:
The white center is now very strong. Black has two main options to counter it.
6...Nc6 attacks the d4 pawn. This pawn cannot be pushed as the e pawn would be left en prise.
6...c5 is far riskier. After 7. d5, Black can be strangled. This game is going to be very tactical.
6...Bf5 is also possible & keeps the option of ...c5 before ...Nc6, but it tends to transpose into 6...Nc6.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 e6 Bg5 dxc4 e4 b5
column3: Black fortifies the c pawn, but allows White to continue with 7. e5. While this may look scary, Black does have a way out.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 e6 e3 Nbd7 Bd3 dxc4
column3: Black captures the c4 pawn with a tempo on White's bishop, forcing White to move it again.\n7. Bxc4 is the only sensible move.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 e3 e6
column3: Black prepares to develop the dark-squared bishop to the b4-square, which was weakened by White's move 5. a4.\nWhite can now simply recapture the c-pawn with 7. Bxc4.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 e3 Na6
column3: This move has a similar idea to the Smyslov variation: to bring the knight to the outpost on b4. White can continue playing in their usual fashion: 7. Bxc4 Nb4 8. O-O e6 9. Qe2, after which White will be able to play e4 without any issues. 9. Ne5 transposes to a line that can be reached from the Krause attack with 6...Na6, as can be seen in Carlsen - Vladimir, 2008.\nThis move was first played by, and named after, Emanuel Lasker in a game against Boris Verlinsky in 1925.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 e6
column3:
Black prepares to develop their dark-squared bishop to b4 where it stands uncontested thanks to White's move 5. a4.
If White tries to recapture the c4 pawn immediately with 7. Nxc4?! Black can strike back 7...c5, putting pressure on White's centre and garnering an advantage in development.
The only move that preserves White's advantage is 7. f3, trying to play e4 on the next move. This threat cannot be stopped by Black, who has to play for piece activity, potentially sacrificing a piece to destroy White's centre.
The Wiesbaden variation is named after the 1929 World Championship match between Alekhine and Bogoljubov. Bogoljubov entered the line in games three and five which took place in Wiesbaden.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 Nbd7
column3: This is a simple developing move. White's only real follow-up is 7. Nxc4, keeping the knights in the center and recapturing the c4 pawn.

column1: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6
column3:
This is the main line of the Queens gambit accepted. With their latest move, Black prepares ...b5 to develop their light-squared bishop. This position is very theoretical, with White having many different ways to respond.
By retreating the light-squared bishop before Black can play ...b5, White can be more flexible in their response to ...b5. The modern main line continues in this fashion: 7. Bb3 keeps the bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal and allows White to immediately attack 7...b5 with 8. a4.
Similarly, the sideline 7. Bd3 allows the same response to 7...b5, but positions the bishop on the b1-h7 diagonal instead.
The move 7. a4 has a simple goal: completely prevent 7...b5. This does leave a hole on b4, which Black can look to exploit with 7...Nc6, aiming for ...Nb4. It is most popular among amateur players, as it allows fairly natural development with Qe2, Rd1 and Nc3.
7. dxc5 exchanges the d-pawn for Blacks c-pawn. This opens up the queens' view of each other, leading to either Black exchanging queens with 7...Qxd1 8. Rxd1 Bxc5, or White initiating the trade after 7...Bxc5 8. Qxd8 Kxd8. This line has by far the most draws out of any of Whites responses, so it is not very ambitious.
7. e4 is the Russian gambit. White gambits the e-pawn with the idea of using the open e-file to attack Blacks king, which is still stuck in the centre. This gambit is completely sound, although the unprepared shouldn't venture into the complications after 7...Nxe4. Instead, Black can deny the gambit with 7...b5, which is also the most popular continuation in the masters database.
7. Qe2 is the old main line. It positions the queen to support the e-pawn to advance, while opening up the d1-square for the rook. It has dropped in popularity over time, and Black equalizes just fine nowadays. The critical continuation begins with the thematic 7...b5, and after 8. Bb3 Bb7 9. Rd1 Nbd7 10. Nc3= the masters database shows Black scoring better than White. In the resulting position, Black has many ways to continue, with White usually following up with either 11. d5 or 11. e4.
7. Re1 is a sideline. The rook supports the e3-e4 advance, while freeing up f1 for the bishop to retreat to.
7. Nc3 is a sideline that also prepares e4, and often transposes into the previous line with 7...b5 8. Bb3 Bb7 9. Qe2. A more independent variation arises after 9. e4 cxd4 10. Nxd4, where the players can once again enter a queenless middlegame after 10...Nc6 11. Nxc6 Qxd1 12. Rxd1 Bxc6.
7. Nbd2 is a sideline which aims to fight for the c4 square with the knight. The knight may sometimes route to b3 too.
7. b3 is a sideline where White tries to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop. While a bishop on c4 and b2 sound great on paper, these majestic bishops get dumbed down after ...b5 is played, forcing the light-squared bishop to the more passive e2-square. This line also results in a draw quite often after 7...cxd4, where White usually recaptures with 8. Nxd4 to keep the a1-h8 diagonal open for the dark-squared bishop.

column1: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 c6 e4 dxe4 Nxe4 Bb4 Bd2 Qxd4
column3: Black takes the gambitted pawn and will be up material for the time being. This opening doesn't come without compensation for White. After 7. Bxb4 White will have dominance over Black's weakened dark squares.

column1: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 h6
column3: Black pushes the bishop away, likely intending to go for either the Tartakower or Lasker's defence.\nApart from White's main option 7. Bh4 they can also avoid these theoretical lines by playing 7. Bxf6.

column1: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 Nbd7
column3:
With this move Black enters the Classical variation. This is an older and well-studied variation that has stood the test of time, as it is still played to this day. Due to its age, White has developed many responses to it over time.
7. Rc1 is the main line, developing the rook to the to-be-opened c-file.
7. Qc2 is the Rubinstein attack. White develops the queen to watch over the b1-h7 diagonal.
7. cxd5 releases the tension from the center and transposes into an exchange variation.
7. Bd3 is the Botvinnik variation, in which Black gains a few tempi on White's bishop with 7...cxd5 and, later on, Nb6.
The classical variation has been played all the way back in the late 1800's and has been deployed by and against the likes of Capablanca, Lasker, Alekhine, Kasparov and many more.

column1: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Be7 Bf4 O-O e3 c5
column3: 6...c5\nBlack immediately strikes the White centre with ...c7-c5. This takes advantage of the Bishop being on f4 instead of g5, which applies less pressure on d5. To demonstrate, after 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Nf3 Be7 5. Bg5 O-O 6. e3 h6 7. Bh4, 7...c5 can be met with 8. Bxf6 Bxf6 9. cxd5 exd5 10. dxc5, and Black is left with a suboptimal isolated queen’s pawn structure.\nWhite’s only move is the Botvinnik exchange: 7. dxc5, forcing the black bishop on e7 to waste a tempo. 7. cxd5 can be met with ...Nxd5, and 7. Bd3 or 7. Be2 can be met with ...dxc4, which all allow black to equalise comfortably.

column1: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 f3 O-O Be3 c5
column3:
This surprising move is one of the biggest questions posed to white's choice of moving the pawn to f3. One of the most interesting and studied gambits in all of chess, the Sämisch Gambit offers a free pawn on c5 to create wild tactical chaos against white's underdeveloped position. White has three main options, according to the masters and the lichess database:
Ignore the pawn break entirely, by developing another piece (Usually Nge2),
Immediately close the center, King's Indian style, with d5,
Or accept the gambit with dxc5 dxc5 Bxc5
The first and second options are probably the best for people who don't want to get into an absolute wilderness of a position. While you miss out on a "free pawn", you can still go ahead with your regular knowledge of the Sämisch, with minimal danger to follow, and as such, they won't be discussed here.
The third option is possibly the most dangerous for both sides. After the pawn is accepted, black immediately brings both knights (Nc6, Ne5, ...) to attack the white king. White tries to either simplify the position or force black's attack to lose its initiative. Lines get extremely complicated after Bxc5, with the engine giving mixed opinions about the gambit.

column1: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 f3 O-O Be3 e5
column3:
This used to be the main line of the Sämisch. Its use has been in steady decline for a while due to 6...c5 becoming the most ambitious way to play the Sämisch variation.
White has the choice to either leave the central tension, or to release it.
7. d5 advances the pawn further into Black's territory. It's presence, however, is only temporary, as Black will be able to get rid of it with 7...c6. This is the main continuation.
7. Nge2 leaves the central tension and prioritizes development instead. While Black has the option of taking the pawn, they often choose to play moves that transpose back into 7. d5 instead.
7. dxe5 releases the tension in the centre and initiates a trade of queens after 7...dxe5 8. Qxd8 Rxd8=.

column1: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5
column3:
This thematic advance 6...e5 from Black attacks the center and gains space. Now White has four options here.
7. O-O is the main move, simply developing and keeping options open. Black’s main response to this is 7...Nc6, luring White to lock the center with 8. d5. After this, we reach the Mar del Plata variation with 8...Ne7, where Black attempts to launch a massive pawn storm starting with ...f7-f5 and checkmate White. White will have to defend precisely here, but will be likely winning if Black runs out of steam.
7. d5, the Petrosian variation immediately locks the center. This also takes away the c6 square for the b8 knight, meaning Black will have to switch their plan here.
7. Be3, the Gilgoric variation simply develops the bishop. However, if Black charges on with a pawn storm like they do in the mainline, White gets an improved version of the Mar del Plata variation where the dark-squared bishop is already developed.
If you want a more simple game, then 7. dxe5, the Exchange variation, is the way to do that. White must be wary of taking the e5 pawn too early, but other than that they should not have issues. Of course, this does not put any pressure on Black.

column1: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7
column3: With this move, Black occupies the long diagonal with their bishop and prepares the vital break ...c5.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5
column3: 6...e5 is the most popular and most unbalancing response to the English attack. The pawn drives off the White's well-placed knight from d4 to a more passive square. Although this creates an outpost on d5, Black is saying, basically, that it is irrelevant to the play on the wings, while White is saying that Black will be lost if d5 is occupied.\nWhite must save their knight, usually to 7. Nb3, and Black's main move is 7...Be6, increasing their control of d5. White's plans include playing f3, Qd2, long castling, and storm on the kingside with pawns.\nLess popular is 7. Nf3, where the threat of Ng5 discourages 7...Be6. The knight prevents f3 and puts the pawn-storm idea on the back-burner. White concentrates on fighting for control of the d5 square instead.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e6
column3: This move order is a common transpositional tool for Scheveningen players to avoid the Keres Attack, which is reached from 6.g4 from a standard Scheveningen position. While it initially follows the Najdorf move order, the e6 push is more characteristic of the Scheveningen than the Najdorf, where black often plays a direct e7-e5 push.\nNote that here, white can choose to follow up with 7. g4, but this line is referred to as the Perenyi Attack rather than the Keres Attack. This is because now that a6 controls the b5 square, black can play 7...e5 without fear of 8.Bb5+. Normally, in the Keres Attack, that would result in a trade of light squared bishops. But in this case, black now has two attackers on the exposed g4 pawn, where there is only one defender, the white queen. Further, 7...e5 threatens the d4 knight, so simply moving 8.h3 to protect the g pawn drops the knight. White's move, therefore, in the mainline Perenyi Attack, is 8.Nf5, cutting off the bishop's assault on g4 while moving the knight to temporary safety.\nWhite can also play the move 7.f3, following the normal English attack plan of castling queenside. The main line is 7...b5 8. Qd2 Nbd7 9.0-0-0 Bb7 10.a3. This is a very sharp line where White wants to attack on the kingside and keep his control of the center, and Black wants to attack on the queenside and break White's central control. The plans usually revolve around White pushing g4 favorably and Black pushing d5 favorably. Whoever does that first without making large concessions is usually better.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 Ng4
column3:
Whereas in the dragon sicilian this move is a blunder, here it is totally safe to play it. The idea is simple: Prevent white from getting the English Attack setup by trading the valuable bishop on e3. There are two main variations:
7. Bc1 is sometimes used to quickly draw the game by repetition, since black wants the bishop and white doesn't give that bishop, repeating moves instead. It is however playable just fine, for example, black can continue with Nf6 Bg5 e6, transposing into another line.
7. Bg5 is the alternative: White wants to place the bishop on g3 and continue the setup normally.
7. Qd2?! allows black to get the bishop pair and gain an extra tempo. White doesn't score as well but it can be a surprise weapon at times.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Be3 Ng4

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6
column3: Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 e6\nWhite's offensive should go on with 7. f4, the most popular move. Queen's moves are also possible as well as 7. Be2 but are considered less ambitious.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 Nbd7
column3: Moves: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 Nbd7\nThis knight move is a natural one in the Najdorf, and it also stops Bxf6, doubling the Black pawns. Although not as popular as the move 6...e6, it is a solid, respectable alternative to the main line. Both sides will usually castle queenside. Black, using his knights and light-squared bishop, will attempt to pressure e4. White, on the other hand, will try to get play on the a2-g8 diagonal and the central files.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7
column3:
7. f3 is the main move. This controls the g4-square and so denies Black ...Ng4, therefore allows White to play Qd2 next and castle long (the Bb5+ idea, which refuted 6...Ng4??, is less powerful now that Black's king can access f8). The pawn on f3 also supports the e4 pawn, liberating the knight from that duty, and can support a king-side pawn storm (g4, h4, g5, h5).
7. Be2 transposes to the classical variation. This allows White to castle short instead, 7...O-O 8. O-O Nc6, with the idea of playing f4 and perhaps e5 (9. Nb3 Be6 10. f4 Qc8 is the Tartakower line), or attacking down the centre with Qd2 and Rad1 (9. Qd2 Bd7 10. Rad1, the battery variation). This sideline is much quieter but has been employed by many players.
7. Qd2!? immediately allows 7...Ng4 8. Bg5 h6 9. Bh4 Nc6, and it is more awkward for White to launch an attack.
7. Bc4 almost always transposes into the old main line following 7...O-O 8. f3 Nc6 9. Qd2.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nb5 d6 c4 Nf6
column3: 6...Nf6 develops while threatening White's e4 pawn.\nWhite can defend with 7. N1c3, developing their second knight and intending their other knight to retreat to a3, or 7. N5c3, leaving their knight on b1 undeveloped for now.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 Be3 Nf6
column3:
Black develops their knight to its natural square where it controls the centre, and prepares to castle.
7. f3?! is the most common move in amateur games, but it is inaccurate. White thinks to play in the manner of the Yugoslav attack, where f3 is necessary to defend e4 and control g4, preventing ...Ng4 and freeing the queen to move to d2. However, in this line, after 7...O-O 8. Qd2, Black has 8...d5!. Compared to the regular dragon, Black saved a tempo by skipping ...d6 and so played ...d5 one turn earlier, before White has had the chance to long castle. White doesn't have the time to deliver their crushing kingside attack and Black has achieved equality.
The modern line is 7. Bc4. By increasing control of d5, White takes the sting out of ...d5 so that they can continue the plan of opposite side castling. It is still possible for White to err in move order here: 7...O-O 8. f3?! is a common inaccuracy on account of 8...Qb6, a double attack on b2 and d4 which threatens the sacrifice ...Nxe4. 8. Be3 must be included to protect b2.
7. Be2, intending 7...O-O 8. O-O, is an alternative. The line continues 8...d5 9. exd5 Nxd5 10. Nxd5 Qxd5 11. Bf3.
7. Nxc6 is another minor side line. This differs from the exchange variation (5. Nxc6) in that White intends 7...bxc6 8. e5, attacking Black's other knight.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6
column3:
Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 6.Ndb5 d6
A little fact that is often forgotten by Sveshnikov players: the d5 square is genuinely weak and likely to remain so. Black's activity doesn't come easy but as compensation for taking on that weakness - an important distinction. White therefore has a logical mini-plan: occupy d5, preferably with a knight, preferably one that can't be instantly captured.
The immediate Nd5 has its followers, as the e-pawn is clearly immune from capture due to Nbc7+. This line was chosen four times by Fabiano Caruana in the World Chess Championship 2018 match against Magnus Carlsen. After Black plays 7...Nxd5, the nice outpost vanishes after 8.exd5 (8.Qxd5 a6 9. Nc3 Be6 is miserable - capturing on d5 with the queen is usually a sign that something's gone wrong). One plan for black is to play 8...Nb8 with ...Nd7 and ...f5 to follow. In their match, Carlsen also tried 8...Ne7 9.c4 Ng6.
White more often pins down the f6 knight with Bg5 - it's important to see this move as a means of increasing control of d5, rather than just pinning a knight out of boredom.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5 cxd5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 Bg5 dxc4
column3: 6... dxc5 results in the classic isolated queen's pawn position. White usually recaptures the pawn, offering up the d pawn for a healthy lead in development, but can also push to d5, or develop the knight to f3.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5 cxd5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 Bg4
column3: White has their eye on the weak points in black's position, b7 and d5, and most commonly takes on d5 with the pawn here. However, 7. Be3, 7. Bg5, and 7. Be2 are also perfectly playable.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6
column3: 7. Nf3 is almost always played, with white aiming to place the knight on e5. White's other options have rarely been seen in master play.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng5 Bg6 N1f3 h6
column3: Black pushes the pawn to kick out the knight. The Knight should now be rerouted to a better square via Nh3-f4.

column1: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4 Kf1 Nc6
column3:
This accurate reply, named the Viennese Variation, deliberately gives up the f7 pawn to attempt to launch an attack on the White king on f1. White has multiple replies to this.
7. Nxf7 seems tempting — it wins the f7 pawn and traps the rook on h8. However, Black can start an attack on White's king with 7...b5! 8. Bb3 (8. Nxh8? bxc4-+ and Black is crushing white despite being down an exchange) Nh6! 9. Nxh8 Bc5! and White's king is struggling to survive.
7. Bxf7+ takes f7 with check but after 7...Kd8 8. d4 Nxe5 9. dxe5 Nh6 10. Bc4 Bc5 11. Qe1 g3! Black has a crushing attack on White's king that is survivable only with precision.
7. Nxc6 gives up the attack on f7 and instead trades knights, but it ruins the Salvio Gambit's idea of saving the knight and allowing Qh4+ to attack f7. After 7...dxc6, Black is better and simply fine.
7. d4 is the most accurate reply, taking the center and defending the knight. Black has a slightly better position after 7...Nxe5 8. dxe5 f3!, where 9. Bf4 is necessary because 9. gxf3?? leads a crushing attack on the White king with 9...Bc5-+.

column1: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4 Kf1 Nh6
column3:
Black chooses to defend f7 using their knight. This opening is called the Silberschmidt Defense. Despite the logicality and popularity of the move, this is not as accurate as the other main replies to 6. Kf1.
7. d4 is what most people play, taking the center and reinforcing the e5 knight. This is usually followed from the Black side by 7...d6 or 7...f3.
7. d3?? simply loses the knight to 7...d6!, trapping it as the d3 square is occupied by the pawn.
7. Nc3 is a minor try where after 7...d6 8. Nd3, Black has a slightly better position but White has more development.

column1: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 O-O gxf3 Qxf3 Qf6
column3:
Black defends their f4 pawn and f7 pawn while developing the queen and blocking the f-file. This is the most testing reply to the Muzio Gambit as it forces White to prove sufficient compensation for the knight sacrifice. Black also carries the threat of 7...Qd4+ winning the bishop on c4. White must not let their attack fizzle out; for example, the most common move at club level is 7. c3, but this is too slow. There are other, better options available for White.
7. d3 is the soundest move for White in this position, but some players consider it slow. It allows the c1 bishop to view the f4 pawn, thus adding another attacker to it.
7. e5 often leads to chaotic play. More common that 7. d3 due to its aggressive style, this often leads to the Double Muzio Gambit, 7...Qxe5 8. Bxf7+, where White sacrifices their bishop as well.
7. Nc3?, the Bello Gambit, tries to distract the queen from defending the f4 pawn by tempting 7...Qd4+, but this simply does not work. After 8. Kh1 Qxc4, White can try either 9. Qxf4 or 9. Nd5 (the Baldwin Gambit), but they can be easily diffused: 9. Qxf4 Bd6-+ or 9. Nd5 d6-+ and Black is up two pieces.
7. b3!? is an extremely rare move which sets a somewhat dastardly trap; 7...Qxa1 8. Nc3 Bg7?? 9. Qxf4! and White is almost completely winning due to the undefendable f7 square and the queen on a1 stuck out of play, not able to do anything.

column1: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4 g4 Ne5 Nf6 Bc4 d5
column3: White's c4-bishop and e4-pawn are forked by the Black pawn on d5. 7. exd5 is necessary to remove the threat.\n7. Bxd5 would be a positional disaster for White. It would give Black a powerful centralised queen after 7...Nxd5 8.exd5 Qxd5, it would bring White no closer to recovering the pawn, and it would give up the bishop pair for no reason. In the analogous position after 7.exd5, 7...Nxd5 would not oblige White to capture the knight.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O b5 Bb3 Bb7
column3:
Black elects to fianchetto his light-square bishop in order to gain pressure against White's kingside and center. This has the added benefit of defending the rook on a8, thereby taking some of the sting out of a future a4 thrust by White. However, the activity of Black's fianchettoed bishop can be countered by White overprotecting e4. Thus the most common reply by White in recent years has been 7. d3, after which Black typically develops his other bishop to either e7 or c5. The latter leads to positions which can also be reached from the Neo-Arkhangelsk (6...Bc5), though 6...Bb7 7. d3 Bc5 is the more common order. With a pawn on d3, White does not need to bring a rook to e1 in the near term, and so his queen's knight often travels to the kingside via c3 (from where d5 also becomes an option) and e2 rather than d2 and f1, since White does not wish to spend a tempo clearing the f1 square.
7. Re1 shares the idea of overprotecting e4 and allows White's queen's knight to take the traditional route; in this variation White intends to forge ahead with c3, d4, and Nbd2-f1-g3, though this knight maneuver will require the insertion of Be3 first if Black's dark-squared bishop has come to the a7-g1 diagonal. If White is not in a rush to develop the queen's knight, his dark-square bishop may instead develop to g5. This line is the oldest variation of the Arkhangelsk, having been played in the 1950 game in which Paul Keres, as black, sprung the then-novel Arkhangelsk on Alexander Kotov.
7. d4 is an old try at immediately refuting Black's move order by preventing an immediate ... Bc5, but after 7...Nxd4, either 8. Nxd4 exd4 or the trickier 8. Bxf7+ Kxf7 9. Nxe5+ Kg8 10. Qxd4 c5 11. Qd1 Qe8 12. Nf3 Qxe4 leaves White with no real advantage.
After 7. c3, Black has scored well playing greedily with 7...Nxe4 8. d4 exd4, though the resulting positions are quite tactically complex. The more common move is 8...Na5.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O b5 Bb3 Bc5
column3: Black wagers that his dark-square bishop is more active here, while his light-square bishop may yet wish to develop along either diagonal. Transpositions to the Old Arkhangelsk (6...Bb7) are common, but there are independent lines involving ...Bg4 as well. White's main ideas in the position are a4, attacking the weak b5 pawn at once, c3 followed by d4, gaining central space and taking a tempo off Black's c5 bishop, or some combination. Also played, but less critical, are 7. Nc3 and 7. d3. The central fork trick 7. Nxe5 leaves white without the prospect of greater central control than his pawn on e4 can provide.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5
column3: Black ends White's pressure on their knight.\n7. Bb3 is necessary to save the bishop.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5
column3:
Black ends White's pressure on the c6 knight.
7. Bb3 is necessary to save the bishop and the typical, automatic move.
From time to time some bright spark will wheel out 7. d5?!, the Richter variation, which can entrap Black if they avoid trading knight for bishop.
7. Nxe5!?, the Friess attack, can lead to a number of trades and an equal position. 7...Nxe5 8. dxe5 bxa4 9. Qd5 Rb8 10. Qxe4.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 exd4
column3:
Black takes on d4 and is temporarily two pawns up, but there is a loose knight sitting on an open file leading straight to their king. This leads to a wellspring of tactics and sharp play for both sides.
7. Re1 pins the knight and threatens to win it. Black must defend it with 7...d5 or 7...f5, and though White is winning the position is very precarious and many natural continuations are blunders.
The line to navigate through the pitfalls is 7...d5 8. Nxd4 (recovers a pawn) Bd6 9. Nxc6 (the natural 9. f3?? Qh4! is a massacre) Bxh2+ 10. Kh1□ (10. Kxh2?? Qh4+ 11. Kg1 and Black has a perpetual check between ...Qf2+ and ...Qh4+) Qh4□ 11. Rxe4+□ (an exchange sacrifice. The tempting 11. Nd4+ leads nowhere, and defending f2 with 11. Be3 is insufficient.) dxe4 12. Qd8+□ Qxd8 13. Nxd8+ Kxd8 14. Kxh2.
7. Nxd4?, recapturing immediately, lets Black off the hook, allowing them to trade the knights and simply be a pawn up. 7...Nxd4 8. Qxd4⩱ and Black's knight on e4 has time to get to safety.
7. c3, the Göring-style move, is just getting silly. This is a mistake as it allows Black's knight to escape while only recovering, at best, one pawn. 7...Nc5! 8. cxd4 Nxa4 9. Qxa4, Black gave back one pawn and ran off with the other and the bishop pair. Even if 7...dxc3? 8. Nxc3? (again Re1 was better) Nxc3!∓ White has traded off a pair of knights and is still two pawns down.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Bxc6 dxc6 O-O Bg4 h3 h5
column3: After h5, black sacrifices the bishop for the betterment of Black's position. 7. hxg4? is bad because after 7. ...hxg4! the knight on f3 is attacked, and moving the knight is even worse. For example, after 8. Nxe5??, white captures the pawn, but  after 8. ...Qh4! the checkmate in four moves is unavoidable. White can also try 7. c3 with the idea of playing d4, but 7. ...Qd3 stops it. 8. hxg4, hxg4. 9. Nxe5, there is a move Bd6, attacking the knight. 10. Nxd3 and then, there is 10. ...Bh2+ and you repeat moves. And white can also play 7. d4 with the idea of developing queenside pieces.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 f5 Nc3 fxe4 Nxe4 d5 Nxe5 dxe4
column3: White ties the minor piece count at 3 with 7. Nxc6. It's a free knight because if Black recaptures with the b-pawn, Bxc6+ followed by Qh5+ gives Black big problems.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bb6 b5 Na5 Nxe5 Nh6
column3: Black defends f7 with their knight and potentially preparing to castle. Most often in amateur play White plays 7. d4, threatening to remove the defender of f7 with Bxh6, however according to Stockfish, 7. Be2 is the best move.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bb6 b5 Na5 Nxe5 Qg5
column3: Black ignores the threat on f7 and instead counterattacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2. White can fork the queen and rook with 7. Nxf7, but runs into complications after 7...Qxg2!. 7. d4 saves the knight but doesn't save g2. Instead, the best move for White is 7. Bxf7+.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 b5
column3: An interesting gambit, Black sacrifices their b7 pawn to White's bishop on c4. The idea is that after 7. Bxb5, Black can play 7...Nxd4 where White's c3 pawn is pinned to the king, and unlike 6...Nxd4?, Nxe5 wouldn't be possible as the bishop on b5 is also attacked.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 d6
column3: A solid move, defending the e5 pawn with their d7 pawn. White usually plays 7. O-O or 7. Qb3. 7. Bg5 is a sideline.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 Nf6
column3: Black counterattacks the e4 pawn with their knight, but this is not good. White should play 7. dxe5 to exploit Black's mistake and set a trap.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4
column3:
The bishop must move, and it did. This is actually the only not losing move. White has a couple options here.
7. Bd2 is a natural blocking move. Black can either trade and break the center with 8...d5, or immediately take with 7...Nxe4 which leads to complicated variations and the sacrifice of 8. Bxf7+!
7. Nc3 is a main line that sacrifices the e4 pawn. This is the Greco Gambit, where White then castles and gambits the pawn for development.
7. Nbd2 also exists. It was once very rare but has recently increased in popularity.
7. Kf1, also known as the Cracow Variation, is not usually played, as White can no longer castle and hangs the e4 pawn. For the pawn, White gains initiative and attacks Black who has to find only moves to keep advantage.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Nxe4 Re1 d5
column3: d5! simultaneously defends the e4-knight and attacks the c4-bishop. However, instead of retreating, White may try the move Bxd5! with hopes of Qxd5 Nc3! attacking the pinned knight on e4 and the queen, and cannot be captured as dxc3?? Qxd5! wins the queen.\nA rarer followup is Nc3!! with the intention of dxc3 Bxd5! winning the knight on e4.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 Bc5 Nxf7 Bxf2 Kxf2 Nxe4
column3: Black plans to bring their queen out with Qh4 next move. To avoid any danger and move out of the open file, White has two sensible options: Kg1 and Ke3.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Nd4 c3 b5
column3: Black kicks White's bishop. This position can also arise from the Ulvestad variation.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Nxd5 d4 Bb4
column3: 6... Bb4+\nBlack tempts the pawn to c3 preventing the White Knight from developing.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Qb6 a3 Nh6
column3: Black develops the knight to h4 intending to manoeuvre it to the f5-square.\n7. Bxh6? attempts to damage Black's pawn structure, but it fails because of 7...Qxb2 threatening to take the rook and only recapturing the bishop after 8. Nbd2. Black ends up being two pawns up in exchange for the slightly damaged kingside, which can be used to attack White with the newly opened g-file.\n7. b4 is the proper response. After which 7...cxd4 8. cxd4 Nf5 places the knight on its target square.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Qb6 Bd3 cxd4
column3: Black trades the pawn on c5 for white's d4 pawn. Black appears to be able to win the pawn but 7.cxd4 Nxd4? 8.Nxd4 Qxd4?? 9.Bb5+ would win the Black queen, so 7...Bd7! is the main move after 7.cxd4. 7.O-O is a modern gambit, sacrificing a pawn for quick development and an attack.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Ba5 b4 cxd4
column3:
By taking on d4, both White's knight and Black's bishop are now hanging. White has two popular responses in this position.
7. Nb5 threatens the d4-pawn and eyes c7. It can potentially move to d6, where it can't be pushed away by pawns. With the bishop still hanging, Black should retreat it. 7...Bb6 protects the d4-pawn, but not d6, where White will be able to put an uncontested knight. Therefore 7...Bc7 is more preferable, gaining a tempo on White's e5-pawn. After 8. f4, protecting the pawn, both sides should do fine with basic developing moves. White does generally exchange the knight for the dark-squared bishop when threatened (after 8...Bd7 9. Nxc7+ for example).
7. Qg4 is more aggressive. White leaves their knight hanging for now, and focuses on attacking Black's kingside, where the bishop is no longer defending. Black can't take the knight, since after 7...dxc3?? 8. Qxg7 Bc7 9. Qxh8 +- White is up a rook and Black's king is in danger.
Instead, Black can respond with either 7...Ne7, playing in a style similar to the poisoned pawn variation, or with 7...Kf8. After 7...Ne7 8. bxa5 dxc3 9. Qxg7 Rg8 10. Qxh7 Nbc6 Black is in a lot of trouble. Black may try to castle queenside, but White has the looming threat of a6, after which Black will have a severely weakened queenside no matter their response.
If 7...Kf8 8. Nb5!? Bb6 and White's knight is placed beautifully on Black's queenside. No matter which way you slice it, the position looks very daunting for Black.
Note that 7. bxa5? isn't great. after 7...dxc3 8. Qg4 Kf8 Black isn't under much pressure at all. If the bishop and the knight had still been there, it would have been much more dangerous for Black.
This variation gets its name from being used by the Armenian grandmasters Rafael Vaganian and Smbat Lputian.
It has, however, been employed quite frequently before attaining this name, becoming popular in the 1950s. It had been deployed most notably in the world championship match between Vasily Smyslov and Mikhail Botvinnik.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Ne7
column3: Black places the knight on its best square.\nAlthough Black's c5 pawn is not defended, White rarely chooses this continuation 7. dxc5, because then White's tripled pawns on the c-file are very weak and Black has an easy time regaining the pawn with 7...Nd7. White's usual continuation from this position is the aggressive 7. Qg4, which threatens to capture Black's undefended g7 pawn.\nAlternatively White can also play the solid 7. Nf3 in order to prepare kingside castling, or they can play 7. a4 with the aim of developing their dark-squared bishop to a3.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Qa5
column3:
Black decides to poke at White's queenside, hoping for them to misplace their pieces. White's best option is to defend the pawn with 7. Bd2.
That is not the end of Black's plan however. After 7...Qa4 Black prevents White from pushing the a-pawn further and tries to keep White's queen stuck defending the c-pawn, though there are still some tricks.
8. Qg4 is the main line. White tries to get Black to weaken their kingside by either forfeiting castling rights with 8...Kf8 or by weakening the dark squares around the king with 8...g6. After either move, White can simply retreat the queen to d1, or play 9. Nf3 to castle kingside quickly. Losing the c2-pawn is usually not a big issue for White because they get a big development lead in return.
8. Qb1 is an alternative, looking for 9. Bb5+ to win the queen. Usually 8...c4 is played to prevent this plan and grab space on the queenside.
Apart from the slightly odd queen placement, Black can usually employ the usual ideas of the Winawer like ...b6 in order to trade off the light-squared bishops. White also has the common idea of h2-h4-h5 to start a king-side attack.
The variation is likely named after the players  Lajos Portisch and William Hook. Hook played this variation against Bobby Fischer who beat him and presumably gave some improvements.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Qc7
column3: Black develops the queen to the c-file, which may be opened up soon with cxd4. However, Blacks kingside still isn't developed, which can be exploited by White.\n7. Qg4 is the main line and Whites most aggressive response. Here we see the second use of Black's previous move: Black can defend the g-pawn with 7...f6 or 7...f5, both of which open up the queens vision of the g-pawn. Alternatively, Black can play 7...Ne7, which transposes into the Poisoned pawn variation.\nWhite can also go for a more positional approach with 7. Nf3, where it is more important to grasp the general ideas of the opening rather than hard lines. White can attack on the kingside with h2-h4-h5, while Black will try to trade the light-squared bishops with b6 followed by Ba6. White generally tries to get as much as possible out of this trade, usually using a combination of Bb5+ and a4 to take back with the a-pawn, placing it on the b5 square to restrict Blacks pieces.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e5 Nfd7 Bxe7 Qxe7
column3:
This is an important branching point in the classical French defence. While the main line 7. f4 occurs in the vast majority of the games, the alternatives are not much worse.
7. f4, the aforementioned main line, has been called the Steinitz variation, though he usually preferred lines such as 4. e5, only playing the move once in his career. After being very rare in the 19th century, the move gradually became dominant over the others during the 20th century.
7. Qd2 is the Rubinstein variation, though it commonly transposes to the 7. f4 line. White seeks to quickly prepare queenside castling. Since queenside castling isn't safe for Black, it is not unlikely to result in a game with opposite side castling and vicious pawn storms on both sides of the board.
7. Nb5 is the Alapin variation. White threatens to fork Black's king and rook on c7. Black will generally at some point spend some tempi to chase the knight away. White will then have the option of rerouting the knight to a3 and subsequently c2, where it supports White's center.
7. Qg4, the Pollock variation, sees White quickly go for a kingside attack with their pieces. While objectively equal according to engine analysis, Black will have to be careful.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 Bd3 c5 c3 Nc6
column3:
Black mounts an attack on the d4 pawn. Currently, they attack it with their c-pawn and their knight on c6, and they can bring another attacker with ...Qb6 should they choose.
White has two main options depending on how they configure their knights, depending on whether they wish to defend the pawn or not.
7. Ngf3, sometimes called the Korchnoi gambit or universal system, adds a defender to the pawn, but means that after 7...Qb6 White cannot bring another defender and the d-pawn is lost. It transpires that this gambit is sound: the continuation is 8. O-O cxd4 9. cxd4 Nxd4 10. Nxd4 Qxd4 11. Nf3 (defends e5 and allows White's queen to defend d3) Qb6, whereupon the choices are 12. Qa4, from where the queen may swing over to the kingside, 12. Qc2, or 12. a3.
7. Ne2 is the main line and traditional way to play. This develops the knight to defend d4 while keeping f3 open for the queen's knight, so if 7...Qb6 8. Nf3 cxd4 9. cxd4 there is no net loss of material.
Black's usual plan is to attack the end of the pawn chain with ...f6. The main continuation is 7...cxd4 8. cxd4 f6 9. exf6 Nxf6.
A final option to defend d4 is 7. Nef3. If 7...Qb6!? 8. Ne2 the line transposes to the 7. Ne2 Qb6!? 8. Nf3 move order. The difference comes after 7...cxd4 8. cxd4 f6 9. exf6 Nxf6, where White has the choice of 10. Ne2 to transpose to the main line or 10. Nh3!?.

column1: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 d6 c4 Nb6 f4 dxe5 fxe5 Nc6
column3: The so-called Alekhine Knights come out to attack White's center, with d4 under attack. White must now defend the pawn. The main line is 7.Be3. 7.Nf3 is strongly met by 7...Bg4 with strong pressure on the center.

column1: a3 e5 b3 d5 c3 Nf6 d3 Nc6 e3 Bd6 f3 O-O g3
column3: White opens the game with a misguided swarm of one-square pawn pushes. However, if Black is not careful, then this barricade of pawns may impede Black's plans.\nWhite's pawn structure inhibits the natural development squares for the knights. In addition, White's king becomes more vulnerable after a potential pawn storm on the kingside, and none of White's pieces can be developed easily lest White pushes a pawn forward, opening up the position.\nThere exists a variation of White's moves with 1. a3 g6 2. b3 Bg7 3. c3 d5 4. d3 c5 5. e3 e5 6. f3 Ne7 7. g3 Nbc6 where Black chooses to maintain an iron grip over the d4-square while freeing the f-pawn to potentially explore pawn breaks on the kingside.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 e6 Bg5 dxc4 e4 b5 e5
column3: White pushes forward the e pawn, attacking the pinned knight. Black can still save the knight by playing 7...h6, kicking away the bishop.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 e6 e3 Nbd7 Bd3 dxc4 Bxc4
column3: White recaptures the pawn.\n7...b5 is the most proper response, justifying the loss of control over the center by making the b7-square available for the light-squared bishop while gaining a tempo.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 e3 e6 Bxc4
column3: White reclaims their lost pawn. Black should follow up with 7...Bb4, pinning White's knight and putting it on a square where it can't be kicked out by pawns.\n7...Nbd7 is also possible, but will most likely transpose back into the main line.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 e6 f3
column3:
White doesn't capture the c4-pawn. Instead, they prepare 8. e4, which comes with tempo on Black's bishop. With the support of the f-pawn, Black can't stop e4 from being played, so they must find an advantage by different means.
7...Bb4 is the main line. This move removes the knight's defence from e4 and has the idea of sacrificing the light-squared bishop on e4 in exchange for three pawns.
