7...c5 tries to disrupt White's centre. After 8. e4 both 8...cxd4 and 8...Bg6 have been tried, but results have generally been favourable for White. This variation was also played in games 3, 5 and 8 of the 2010 World Chess Championship.
Modern engines prefer the move 7...Bg6, but this is rarely played and usually transposes after 8. e4 c5.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 Nbd7 Nxc4
column3: White recaptures the c4 pawn.\nBlack can now choose to either enter the Carlsbad variation with 7...Qc7 or to transfer the knight to b6 with 7...Nb6.

column1: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 c6 e4 dxe4 Nxe4 Bb4 Bd2 Qxd4 Bxb4
column3: White takes Black's dark-squared bishop. White's dark-squared bishop is now placed on a very active diagonal, cutting through d6, e7 and f8. Black should play 7...Qxe4+ to not be down a piece.

column1: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Be7 Bf4 O-O e3 c5 dxc5
column3: 7. dxc5\nWhite captures the c-pawn with 7. dxc5, forcing the black bishop on e7 to waste a tempo with 7...Bxc5. Note that 7...dxc4 leads to a favorable endgame for white after 8. Bxc4 Qxd1+ 9. Rxd1, where white enjoys more active pieces.

column1: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 O-O
column3:
7. 0-0
White simply develops here, keeping the tension in the center, which is the main move.
Black’s main move here is 7...Nc6, provoking White into closing the center with d5. Then, the knight is routed to e7 where it can support f5. A sharp game will ensue where Black will try to launch a vicious attack on White's king.
7...Nbd7, the old mainline, 7...Na6, the Glek defense and 7...a5, the Ukrainian Defense all share the idea of meeting d4-d5 by planting a knight on c5, and preventing b4 with ...a5
7...exd4 is a sideline, leading to positions where White has a typical Maroczy bind against a kingside fianchetto.

column1: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Bc4
column3: This move places the bishop on a good, active post. However, the drawback is that Nf3 will become unplayable, since Bg4! will put unbearable pressure on d4. It's either Be2/Nf3, Bc4/Ne2 or Bc4/Nf3/h3. In this setup, the bishop will be more active, while in the other setup, the knight will be so. That other setup has increasingly popular since the 1980's.

column1: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Nf3
column3: This move starts a piece setup that has become increasingly popular since the 1980's. White moves their knight to an active place. The drawback is that the bishop will have to settle for the passive e2-square, else Bg4 would be strong.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5 Nb3
column3:
White saves their knight. Black now needs to develop their pieces.
They usually begin 7...Be6, which increases their control of the d5 square, a potential outpost for White, while eyeing White's queenside (where Black anticipates White may castle). White continues 8. f3, preventing ...Ng4 and preparing to attack on the kingside with a brute-force pawn storm and long castling. This might take the form 8...Be7 9. Qd2 O-O 10. O-O-O Nbd7 11. g4. If Black obstructs those plans, as with 8...h5 to prevent g4, White switches tack to prioritise the skirmish for d5 and fight in the centre instead.
7...Be7 is another move-order, and is good as long as Black intends to follow up with ...Be6.
The knight is developed later, after the queen's bishop is developed and ...Nbd7 won't block it in. (...Nc6 is contraindicated: as Black may want use of the half-open c-file and the knight may need to route to b6 to control d5 and c4).

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e6 g4
column3: The Perenyi Attack is similar in idea to its cousin the Keres Attack of the standard Scheveningen Variation. White mounts an aggressive pawn storm on the kingside, castling long and supporting with Be3 and Qd2. However, it usually arises from a transposition from the Najdorf rather than the normal Scheveningen move order. Compared to the Keres, white has his bishop already developed to the e3 square while black has a pawn on a6 rather than a7.\nThe differences are subtle but critical. Now, the standard line of the Perenyi attack follows with 7...e5. This puts two attackers on the advanced g4 pawn (which only has the queen defending) and threatens the d4 knight. If this were the Keres, white could play the intermediate sequence 7. Bb5+ Bd7 8. Bxd7+ Qxd7, eliminating black's light squared bishop, a potential defender of the weak d5 square, and removing the guard from the f6 knight. White then continues with 9. Nf5, getting the knight out of danger and cutting off the queen's attack on the g4 pawn. Here, black would love to play 9...g6, chasing away the knight and then grabbing the g4 pawn, but it doesn't work. White could respond with either 10. Bg5, counterattacking the now undefending f6 knight, or 10. Ne3, defending the g4 pawn, and increasing white's hold on d5.\nHowever, 8. Bb5+ is not an option here because of the a6 pawn. Therefore, white usually plays 8. Nf5, with the same idea of saving both the the knight and the g4 pawn. But here black plays the critical line 8...g6, which comes with much greater effect in this version, since now neither of the above-mentioned resources from the Keres attack are available. The knight on f6 is protected by the queen, so 9. Bg5 is ineffective, and 9. Be3 is impossible, since that square is occupied by white's bishop. At this point, play becomes very complex and sharp. White cannot move the knight away without losing the g4 pawn, and so usually chooses to sacrifice it. White can try to win back a knight with 9.g5 gxf5 10.gxf6, or sacrifice it with 9.g5 gxf5 10.exf5 Ng8 11.f6, boxing in black's kingside pieces. Alternatively, white can develop with 9.Bg2. This leads to a very complex line mostly found in top level chess: 9...gxf5 10. exf5 d5 11. Qe2 d4 12. O-O-O.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4
column3:
Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4
Again, Black has to make a strategic choice. Common moves are :
7...Be7
7...Qc7
7...Nbd7
Two very sharp variations are seen at higher levels : 7...Qb6 (the Poisoned Pawn Variation) and 7...b5 (the Polugaevsky Variation).

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3
column3:
White's f-pawn defends e4, freeing the c3-knight from the duty, and controls the g4-square. This prevents ...Ng4, which Black was threatening to play and gain time on White's bishop. The pawn on f3 is critical for supporting a king's side attack with g4, h4, and h5 in the future, where White aims to take advantage of the "hook" in the Black king's side, the g6 pawn.
7...O-O is the main move, which gets the king to safety, and aims to setup a sharp and exciting game involving opposite-sides castling.
7...Nc6 is the Belezky line. Usually this is just a small move order difference, and transposes to the main line after 8. Qd2 O-O. However, seeing that White is already preparing to storm the king's side, Black's idea may be to avoid castling completely.
7...a6!? is an alternative. The move ...a6 on turn five is the start of the Najdorf variation, so this line that mixes the Najdorf with the dragon is given the twee name dragondorf. That's where the similarities end, though: the usual way of combatting the English attack (the Yugoslav's cousin in the Najdorf) involves ...e5 and ...Be6, where ...a6 serves to prevent Nb5 or Bb5+, but a pawn on e5 is hardly desirable in the Dragon with Black's bishop on g7. Instead the idea of ...a6 in the dragondorf is usually to support ...b5, and Black plays with a queen's side fianchetto and avoids castling.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nb5 d6 c4 Nf6 N1c3
column3: 7. N1c3 defends White's e4 pawn while developing their knight.\nBlack usually continues 7...a6, compelling White to retreat to the passive a6 square. However, at least from there White will overprotect the c4 pawn and keep d5 in sight of their queen.\nBlack can delay a6 until after they have castled: 7...Be7 8. Be2 9. O-O O-O 10. a6.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 c4 Bg7 Be3 Nf6 Nc3
column3: Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3\n7...Ng4: Breyer Variation

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 Be3 Nf6 Bc4
column3:
This is the main line. White develops their bishop and increases control of d5 before playing f3. This prevents Black's rejoinder 8...d5, that otherwise equalises against the move order 7. f3 O-O 8. Qd2.
After 7...O-O, the main move, White must first move their bishop again, 8. Bb3, before continuing with f3 (controlling g4), Qd2, and O-O-O. Otherwise, 8. f3?! is answered with 8...Qb6!, 8. Qd2? with 8...Ng4!, exposing an attack on d4 while attacking White's dark square bishop.
7...Qa5!? is a sideline. This compels White to give up on the idea of long castling.
The immediate threat is that 7...Qa5 pins the knight, so 8. Qd2? hangs the e-pawn. 8...Nxe4 9. Nxc6 Qxc3 10. Qxc3 Bxc3+ 11. bxc3 dxc6 ∓.
8. f3 Qb4 threatens to take the bishop. 9. Bb3 Nxe4! and it turns out the f-pawn wasn't enough to protect the e-pawn, as Black has now unleashed three attacks on d4. 10. fxe4? Bxd4 11. Bxd4 Qxd4 12. Qf3 ∓.
8. Nb3 attacks the queen, but can also be met with 8...Qb4 threatening to take the bishop. The line may continue e.g. 9. Nd2 Qxb2 10. Nb5 Qe5 ∓.
Therefore White's best play is 8. O-O, unpinning the knight and defending the e-pawn. If Black continues with 8...Qb4?! anyway, then 9. Qe2 defends the bishop and the b-pawn is poisonous. (9...Qxb2 10. Ncb5 Nxe4 11. Rab1 Nc3 12. Rxb2 Nxe2+ 13. Bxe2 +-.)
Alternatively 7...d6 transposes into the regular dragon variation.
This line was popularised in the 1950s. One of the most famous games in this position is Fischer v. Reshevsky, 1958. After 7...O-O 8. Be3!, Reshevsky thought to trade off the bishop with 8...Na5?, and ran afoul of 9. e5 Ne8?? 10. Bxf7+ Kxf7 11. Ne6 dxe6 12. Qxd8 +-. The game, which Chess Life described as "sensational", served Reshevsky his only loss in the tournament and clinched the US chess championship title for Fischer.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5
column3: Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 6.Ndb5 d6 7. Bg5\nPinning the knight on f6 is whites main continuation in this line. This increases the pressure on d5 by taking one of the defenders out and also protects the e4 pawn, which is very important if the knight on c3 gets driven away by blacks b-pawn.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nc3 e6 g4 Bg6 Nge2 c5 h4
column3: Black must save the bishop, and their most active response is 7... h5. At first 7... h6 looks preferable, as after 8. Nf4 it allows the bishop to retreat and the pawn to be safe, but Black can safely give up the h pawn in exchange for counterplay on the queenside.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3
column3: The white knight on e5 is usually seen as too powerful, and black normally chooses Nd7 to prevent this.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng5 Bg6 N1f3 h6 Ne6
column3: Like the Alien Gambit, the Martian Gambit leads to an interesting and very exciting game. White plays Ne6, which is considered a blunder by Stockfish. However, in a real game, the move does pretty well. It ruins the kingside, doubles Black's pawns, and what is most important, helps the knight on f3 to deploy on e5 and control king's escape squares. But don't fret, Black has various responses to this gambit.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3
column3:
Black is no longer under any direct threat and may continue to develop. The king and c8-bishop still need to find better squares.
Of the three natural moves, 7...Bb7, the Trajković counterattack, is considered a sideline as it gives up the option of ...Bg4. White usually spends a tempo on h3 to prevent ...Bg4, and this move order lets White spend that tempo elsewhere. If Black's going to put this bishop on b7 early on, they normally want to have the other bishop on c5.
The main moves both carry threats of different types.
7...d6 is the main line. The d-pawn defends the e5-pawn a second time, freeing the c6-knight to come to a5 and swap off White's precious bishop. Therefore it "forces" the move 8. c3―a move White wants to play anyway―to give the bishop an escape square while preparing to advance the d-pawn. The main line continues 8...O-O 9. h3 and reaches a very theoretically rich position where Black has half a dozen serious continuations.
7...O-O first allows Black to follow up with the Marshall gambit 8. c3 d5!?. Black still has the option of 8...d6, and since in modern times 7...d6 is almost always followed by 8...O-O anyway, at first glance it seems that 7...O-O is a clear winner over 7...d6 in terms of giving Black options. That can't be entirely true, or no-one would play 7...d6. Firstly, the Marshall gambit has been analysed to death, and if there's a way of proving it absolutely sound it hasn't been discovered yet. Secondly, White has a choice of ways of dodging it: 8. h3, steering the game back towards the main line, or 8. a4, eliminating the need to play c3.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3
column3:
White brings their bishop away from danger. It is well placed on the a2-g8 diagonal. Now White is threatening dxe5 to recapture the pawn. Rather than be greedy, Black should allow White to take the pawn back and focus on improving their own position instead.
White also has another threat. Three of Black's pieces are aligned on the same diagonal, and many amateur games have run afoul of ideas involving Bd5!, attacking both knights and pinning the knight on c6 to the rook on a8. If Black underestimates this danger they can lose quickly. Not uncommon in amateur databases are:
7...exd4?, thinking that trading is good when one is up material, makes the mistake of opening the e-file before Black has castled, and White is ready to exploit it. One line is 8. Re1 (pinning the knight) d5 9. Nc3!, threatening Bxd5, where 9...dxc3? 10. Bxd5! anyway.
7...d6??, thinking to defend the pawn on e5, allows 8. Bd5! immediately.
7...Na5? walks into either 8. Bd5! or  8. Bxf7+! Kxf7 9. Nxe5+ Kg8 10. Qf3.
7...Nxd4? is refuted by 8. Nxd4 exd4? 9. Bd5!.
As there is no good way to prevent dxe5 or hold onto the pawn (we've looked at 7...exd4? and 7...d6?; of course 7...f6? and 7...Qf6? are no good either), Black should give it back and make an improving move.
7...d5 is far and away the main move. This move should be foremost in Black's mind: it takes space, it fortifies the knight on e4, it limits the scope of the bishop on b3 (the d5 square is now defended by Black's queen), and it affords Black some flexibility in the development of the back rank.
7...Be7 is the only alternative to consider, but after 8. dxe5 it is too late to play ...d5. 8...O-O 9. Bd5 Nc5, gives White the space and an easier time completing their development.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 d5
column3:
White leaves their bishop en prise to counterattack Black's knight instead.
Black can rescue the knight 7...Ne7 and it seems then White must play 8. Bb3 anyway. However, White has the devious move 8. Re1!, where the natural move 8...Nc5?, which preserves the knight and prepares to trade off the bishop, is an error: 9. Nxe5 bxa4?? 10. Qf3! threatens 11. Qxf7#. 10...f6? 11. Qh5+!.
In actual fact, allowing the trade of knight for bishop (either knight, 7...Ne7 8. Re1 bxa4 or 7...bxa4 8. dxc6) is fine for Black:
After 7...bxa4 8. dxc6 d6, forget about Black's potentially slightly rubbish rook pawns, one of which is an extra pawn anyway. Black has a stable centre, a half-open b-file, a kingside pawn majority that could quite easily wallop White after ...f5 and ...Nf6 and the bishop pair: it's one of those rare positions that are just really good fun (your mileage may vary).

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 f5 Nc3 fxe4 Nxe4 d5 Nxe5 dxe4 Nxc6
column3:
Black's queen is attacked, and capturing the attacker with 7...bxc6 will end in tears after 8.Bxc6+ Bd7 9.Qh5+! So we have to move the queen. Moving the queen to the fourth rank seems like a good idea, to try and neutralise the discovered check by hitting the b5-bishop, and at the same time cut out any of White's Qh5+ ideas.
Sure enough, the two variations from this position are both queen moves to the fourth rank:
7...Qg5 is the Classical Variation. The queen counter-attacks the helpless g2-pawn.
7...Qd5 is the Möhring Variation. The queen threatens the bishop and, indirectly, the knight with capture. White's only move to hold things together will be 8.c4, after which Black can argue that White's d-pawn is backward on an open file. Whether this is actually relevant with so many tactical possibilities on the board is another matter.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 d6 Bg5
column3: An interesting sideline, White develops their c1 bishop and attacks Black's queen on d8. Black can choose from 7...Nge7, 7...Qd7, 7...f6 or 7...Nf6.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4 Kf1
column3:
This is a weird-looking move that seemingly doesn't make any sense. White can no longer castle and the e4 pawn is undefended. But the compensation exists. White has got a massive center while Black has none, and White are more prepared to attack than Black. The Cracow Variation a tricky opening, Black has to find the only moves to not to get a bad position. Black has several options:
7...Nxe4. Black has grabbed an actually free pawn. White can strike in the center with 8. d5!, kicking the knight back. After 8...Ne7 White has 9. Qd4, grabbing even more space, or a tricky 9. Bb3 with a threat of 10. Qd4 which is somewhy often unseen.
7...d5!. This is the strongest for Black option. After 8. exd5 Nxd5 9. Nc3 Black has to be careful to not to take the knight with their own knight. There is no reason to trade off a central knight. None. Instead, they should take the knight with the bishop, like in the Greco Gambit.
7...O-O?. After 8. d5! Black has giant problems with space and activity. In case of 8...Ne7 or 8...Nb8 White will go 9. e5!, completely paralysing Black, in case of 8. Na5 there is 9. Bd3 with an unstoppable 10. a3 and 11. b4.
7...d6??. This is a blunder. After 8. d5! Ne7 or 8...Na5 there is 9. Qa4+, winning the bishop on b4.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4 Nc3
column3: This is the traditional way to block the bishop check. With 7. Nc3, white does sacrifice the e4 pawn, but aims to get a dangerous initiative

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Nxe4 Re1 d5 Bxd5
column3: White plays the astounding Bxd5!! which seems to blunder a bishop. However, after Qxd5, Nc3! takes advantage of the two heavy piece pins and wins back the piece with a fork.\nThe only (natural) followup is 7...Qxd5.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 Bc5 Nxf7 Bxf2 Kxf2 Nxe4 Ke3
column3: This is the move which modern chess engines prefer.\nBlack continues their plan with Qh4.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Na5 Bb5 c6 dxc6
column3: This inflicts isolated pawns on Black after the usual response 7...bxc6. 7...Nxc6 is playable but very rare as it does not gain a tempo on White's bishop.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxf7 Kxf7 Qf3
column3: White gives check and attacks the Knight. Black's king has several moves, but only one of them is good. The worst is         7...Kg8?? which loses to 8. Bxd5+ Qxd5 9. Qxd5+ Be6 10. Qxe6# (or 8. Qxd5+ Qxd5 9. Bxd5+ Be6 10. Bxe6#).  7...Ke8? doesn't work because of 8. Bxd5. Black has to defend the knight with Ke6.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Qb6 Bd3 cxd4 cxd4
column3: This is an obvious recapture and it also sets a devious trap! If black continues 7... Nxd4? 8. Nxd4 Qxd4??, 9. Bb5+ wins the queen.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Ne7 Nf3
column3: By developing the knight, White takes on a more positional approach. Because this move is less confrontational than 7. Qg4, Black has more options for dealing with it.\n7...Bd7 threatens to put the bishop on a4, where it puts lasting pressure on White's c2-pawn. White usually prevents this with 8. a4. The drawback of placing the bishop on d7 is that the b-knight can no longer occupy that square, making dxc5 possible. This isn't too big of a deal, since it allows 8...Ba4 after which the knight can go to d7 and recapture the pawn.\n7...b6 intends to trade off the light-squared bishops. White can prevent this trade with 8. Bb5+ Bd7 9. Bd3 but Black gets 9...Ba4 in. If White wants to prevent Ba4 they can play 8. a4 but this does allow Black to trade bishops with 8...Ba6. White can make things slightly more difficult for Black by not exchanging the bishops on Black's terms and playing 9. Bb5+ Bxb5 10. axb5.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Ne7 Qg4
column3:
By playing 7. Qg4, White immediately attacks Black's unprotected g7 pawn.
Now it's Black's choice whether they want to defend the pawn, e.g. by playing 7...O-O or 7...Kf8, or whether they're
going to sacrifice the g7-Pawn and prepare some counterplay on the queenside instead. For this purpose
Black can try 7...Qc7, the Poisoned Pawn variation. This variation can also be transposed into via 7...cxd4.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 Bd3 c5 c3 Nc6 Ne2
column3:
7. Ne2 defends the d-pawn while keeping the f3 square open for White's other knight. This means that 7...Qb6 8. Nf3 and Black doesn't have sufficient attackers to win the d-pawn.
White controls a lot of space. If Black plays a passive move, like 7...a5 or 7...Be7, White can play 8. f4 (there are other good moves), securing their space advantage.
The pawn chain is a nuisance for Black and they should like to find a way to break it down. Unable to win the d-pawn, Black must attack the end of the pawn chain with ...f6, and make progress towards improving their position that way. But first, Black must resolve the tension around d4.
7...f6?! immediately is inaccurate. Rather than answer 8. exf6, White has the option of 8. Nf4! (8. f4! is also good) threatening Nxe6 and Qh5+ to exploit Black's weakened kingside and king, who is still in the centre. Now 8...cxd4? is too late (9. Nxe6! Qb6 10. Qh5+ etc.). 8...Qe7 is the best try. (9. Nf3 fxe5 10. dxe5 Ndxe5 11. Nxe5 Nxe5 seems to win a pawn until 12. Qh5+! Nf7 13. Bxh7!! intending 14. Ng6 trapping the rook.)
7...cxd4 is a useful inclusion for several reasons. One is that it releases squares on the queenside where Black might like to put their knight or bishop, another is that it increases pressure on d4, because after 7...cxd4 8. cxd4 (8. Nxd4? drops the e-pawn), Black's pressure keeps White's knight tied down to defend d4.
After 8...f6, the main move, 9. Nf4? does not work because of this pressure. Black has 9...Nxd4! which defends e6. To prevent ...fxe5 White has to play 9. exf6, which allows Black to improve their position with 9...Nxf6. The main line continues 10. Nf3 Bd6 11. O-O, and either 11...O-O 12. Bf4 to trade off Black's good bishop, or 11...Qc7 12. Bg5.
An alternative is 8...Qb6 9. Nf3 (or in the order 7...Qb6 8. Nf3 cxd4 9. cxd4). Black's queen pressures b2, but in many of these lines the pawn is poisonous and White can move the queen's bishop away, sacrifice both the b-pawn and more, and still come out ahead due to initiative generated on the open queenside.
9...Qb4+?! 10. Bd2! Qxb2 11. Rb1 Qxa2 (Black is two pawns up) 12. Nc3 attacks the Queen, and
12...Qa5 13. Nb5 (discovered attack on queen and threatens Nc7+) Qd8 14. Ng5± with ideas like Nxe6, Qh6.
12...Qa3 and there is the extraordinary sequence 13. Nb5 (threatening Nc7+ but hanging a bishop?) Qxd3 14. Nc7+ Kd8 15. Nxe6+!! (not 15. Nxa8?) fxe6 16. Bg5+ Kc7 17. Qxd3+-.
Since the b-pawn is often poisonous, the continuations are
9...Bb4+ 10. Bd2 and White is happy to trade off Black's good bishop;
9...f6 10. exf6 Nxf6 11. O-O Bd6.
7. Ne2 was traditional line popular in the 19th century. It is still the mainline today, though 7. Ngf3 has gain ground as a playable alternative.
Siegbert Tarrasch v Karl Eckart, Nuremburg 1889.
1. e4 e6 2. d4 d5 3. Nd2 Nf6 4. e5 Nfd7 5. Bd3 c5 6. c3 Nc6 7. Ne2
The main line of the Closed Tarrasch variation of the French defence. White reserves the f3 square for their queen side knight.
7...Qb6 8. Nf3 Be7
Defending d4 with both knights and the pawn prevents Black from winning the pawn, however it is still a useful, freeing move to liquidate the c-pawns with 8...cxd4 9. cxd4. If nothing else, Black's bishop would have had more scope and could have developed more actively to 8...Bb4+.
9. O-O O-O 10. Nf4
White is allowed to keep the space on the kingside and can bring their pieces into a crushing attack. Black's position is too passive and their pieces too far from the king to protect it.
11..Nd8 11. Qc2
Threatens 12. Bxh7+.
11...f5?! 12. exf6 e. p. Nxf6
Black hopes forcing White to give up the f-pawn and letting them get their knight to defend the kingside will be enough, but unfortunately this takes the e7 bishop out of the defence.
Better was 11...g6 12. h4 f5 13. exf6 Rxf6.
13. Ng5
Threatens 14. Bxh7+ again.
13...g6 14. Bxg6 hxg6?? 15. Qxg6+ Kh8 16. Qh6+ Kg8 17. Ng6
18. Qh8# to follow. Black resigns 1-0.

column1: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 d6 c4 Nb6 f4 dxe5 fxe5 Nc6 Be3
column3: With this move, White defends the d4-pawn with the bishop while not allowing the ...Bg4 pin. Black now almost always plays 7...Bf5, since that is the only logical square for the bishop. Then White plays 8.Nc3 and then Black plays 8...e6, and now White plays 9.Nf3 when Black has a choice between several moves.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 e6 Bg5 dxc4 e4 b5 e5 h6
column3: This is the only move for Black to not lose a piece. White's main response is 8. Bh4, retreating the bishop and retaining the pin.\nThe alternatives to 8. Bh4 give Black relatively little problems. If White tries 8. exf6? Black gets a comfortable position up a pawn after 8...hxg5 9. fxg7 Bxg7.\n8. Bxf6?! is also dubious at best and allows Black to quickly equalize. Since White has given up the dark-squared bishop, Black can combat White's remaining bishop by putting the majority of their pawns on light squares.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 e6 e3 Nbd7 Bd3 dxc4 Bxc4 b5
column3:
Black expands on the queenside and makes the b7-square available for their bishop while gaining a tempo on White's bishop.
White should retreat the bishop, there are three viable options:
8. Bd3 is the main line, returning the bishop to the square it was originally positioned on. From this square, it supports the e4 pawn-push and glances at Black's kingside.
8. Be2 is a more passive option. It can't be attacked as easily on e2 as on d3, but its also not as active in the attack.
8. Bb3 is the most aggressive option, keeping the bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal. White can generate a lot of pressure on the e6 and f7 pawns, possibly sacrificing a knight for the initiative. This option is not guaranteed if Black knows the theory well, so Black can come out with a slight edge if they are well prepared.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 e3 e6 Bxc4 Bb4
column3: Black develops the bishop to its most natural square.\nWhite should simply castle kingside 8. O-O to get out of the pin and start preparing e4.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 e6 f3 Bb4
column3:
Black makes use of the weakened b4-square, pressuring the knight on c3 and gaining a bit more control over e4.
The main line continues with 8. e4, also known as the Sharp line. Black has to sacrifice their light-squared bishop for three pawns if they want to retain any winning chances.
8. Nxc4 is White's main alternative, avoiding many of the complications that ensue from 8. e4. The position branches out after Black castles.
8. Bg5 is a rare continuation that has lost it's popularity over time. Usually Black responds with 8...h6, which gives their light-squared bishop a nicer square to go to if e4 happens.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 Nbd7 Nxc4 Qc7
column3: Black develops the queen to c7 in order to prepare e5. This will likely lead to the Carlsbad variation.\nWhite's main response is 8. g3 preparing to develop the dark-squared bishop to f4 where it can put pressure on the knight after 8...e5 9. dxe5 Nxe5. This also prepares to fianchetto the light-squared bishop.

column1: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 c6 e4 dxe4 Nxe4 Bb4 Bd2 Qxd4 Bxb4 Qxe4
column3: Black recaptures the piece. This is the starting point of the Marshall gambit. White has two main ways of blocking the check, both leading to complex positions where White has to find a way to convert their lead in development into a tangible advantage. White should generally avoid trading pieces, especially queens, as any endgame will favour Black.\n8. Be2 is the main line, blocking the check with the bishop. This leaves the g2-pawn undefended, but taking it would be unwise, since it allows White to develop even more quickly with Bf3, Ne2 and then Rg2 comes with tempo.\n8 Ne2 is less popular, but still very often played. This leaves the c4-pawn undefended, but taking it is once again way too dangerous for Black because of Qd6!, infiltrating on the weakened dark squares. The main continuation in this line ends up restoring material equality.

column1: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 h6 Bh4 b6
column3: 7...b6 enters the Tartakower defence, where Black hopes to develop the light-squared bishop. While it looks like Black intends to fianchetto the bishop, this isn't necessarily true. If White tries to blunt the a8-h1 diagonal immediately with 8. cxd5, Black will nonetheless be able to develop the bishop: 8. cxd5 Nxd5 9. Bxe7 Qxe7 10. Nxd5 exd5 = and Black can now put the bishop somewhere on the c8-h3 diagonal instead (usually going to e6).

column1: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 h6 Bh4 Ne4
column3: Black centralizes the knight, opening up an attack on White's dark-squared bishop.\nThe mainline continues by trading the dark-squared bishops and later the knights as well.

column1: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Be7 Bf4 O-O e3 c5 dxc5 Bxc5
column3: 7...Bxc5\nBlack recaptures the pawn. Now White can play the unambitious 8. cxd5 and saddle black with an isolani, or continue going down the rabbit hole with the mainline 8. Qc2, where the queen points towards the black kingside. It should be noted that 8. a3 transposes into the mainline.

column1: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 O-O Nc6
column3: 7...Nc6\nThe main move for Black. This pressures the d4 pawn, so White is forced to play 8. d5. This technically gets a tempo on the knight, but White has now locked the center. Also, the knight can then go to e7 and support the ...f7-f5 pawn break. A sharp game will ensue.

column1: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Bc4 c5
column3: This pawn lever also tries to attack the center. Since the center is potentially opening, white is well advised to move his king out of danger with 8.Ne2 followed by O-O.

column1: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Nf3 c5
column3: This move is the key pawn lever, taking advantage of the diagonal. Note that the long diagonal is weak. Without this lever, d4 would be indestructible and the Grünfeld defence would be unsound. White has four main moves, the most theoretical being 8. Rb1.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5 Nb3 Be6
column3: Moves: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Be3 e5 7.Nb3 Be6\nThis is the best move. The Black bishop covers d5 from e6 and also points at the queenside when White castles there. Black also contemplates using c4 as a piece outpost. Black's position retains maximum flexibility, as in almost all variations Black plays ...Be7, ...Nbd7, ...O-O, ...Rc8, and ...Nb6 in some order.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 b5
column3:
Moves : 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6. Bg5 e6 7. f4 b5
White has several possible choices. Common moves are :
8. e5 (main line)
8. Qf3
8. a3

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 Be7
column3: Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 Be7\nThis used to be the main line, mostly out of Fischer's theoretical work. Today it is considered the sharpest line, with sacrifices on d5, b2, g7, and f7, and other such things. Mostly it is because of the large mass of variations that stem from this position. Today, however, the variation has rather fallen out of favor due to the increasing popularity of the Poisoned Pawn Variation after 7...Qb6.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 Qb6
column3: Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 Qb6\nBlack launches a direct attack on the b2 pawn. White should defend it with 8. Nb3 or leave it to the enemy with 8. Qd2. This variation gained notoriety in the 1960s with Fischer's espousal of the system. His idea was that after grabbing a pawn, he could use his almost flawless technique to neutralize White's dangerous lead in development, and then win with his extra pawn and bishop pair.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 Nc6
column3: The Belezky Line is a Yugoslav Attack sideline where black plays Nc6 instead of castling. White may continue with 8. Bc4, also trying to develop all their pieces before castling. This may be used as a weapon to make white question if black is going to castle at all.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 O-O
column3: The Yugoslav Attack continues with 7...O-O. In the Yugoslav, Black castles kingside while White castles queenside, leading to an opposite-side-castling game where speed is important. Black often pushes on the queenside with a5 and b5 and continues advancing those pawns, while White plays g4 and h4 and continues advancing those pawns. The fianchettoed bishop on g7 is a key piece in Black's attack on the queenside and what makes the Dragon the Dragon.\nWhite's most popular continuation is 8. Qd2, preparing for a queenside castle.\nSecond is 8. Bc4, which often transposes to the main line.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nb5 d6 c4 Nf6 N1c3 a6
column3:
7...a6 kicks White's knight.
Its available squares are d4 or a3.
The most common move is 8. Na3. This places a knight on the rim, but at least it overdefends c4 in case Black hopes to make use of the half-open file and play ...Rc8 one day.
8. Nd4 reduces White's control of d5, and allows Black to untangle with 8...d5 9. cxd5 exd5 10. exd5 Nxd5 11. Nxc6 bxc6= (see diagram). The position is equal but now open, and White is no longer able to keep Black suffocating in their side of the board as they had hoped.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 c4 Bg7 Be3 Nf6 Nc3 Ng4
column3: Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 Ng4\nThis opening is ECO code B39.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6
column3: The primary purpose of 7...a6 is to drive the knight on b5 away from its strong position. The knight on b5 threatens to jump to c7, which would be a fork on Black's king and rook, and puts pressure on d6. By pushing the a-pawn, Black gains space on the queenside, which can support further pawn advances like ...b5, potentially leading to active counterplay on that side of the board. Forcing the knight to retreat diminishes White's immediate threats and allows Black to better organize their pieces. The knight typically moves to a3, where it is less active compared to b5.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7
column3: 8. h5 is mostly played, aiming to tie up black's kingside pawns. The pawn on h5 is double-edged. It's powerfully positioned in black's territory, but it also requires protection from the knight on g3, making this potentially a bad piece.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6
column3: Whenever White opens with 1. e4, her most reliable plan is then to prepare to play d4. There is a very good reason not to play 8. d4? instantly - click and learn.\nInstead, it must be prepared with 8. c3. With White's kingside fully developed there is no reason to delay this useful move any longer.\nNote that h3 will be a useful move, but not yet - because it turns out that 8. c3 is also necessary to give the b3-bishop a retreat square. A White player who forgets her move order and plays 8. h3 is liable to have her bishop confiscated with 8...Na5.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O
column3:
White's natural move in this position is
8.c3, continuing with the plan of eventually playing d4. This invites the Marshall Gambit ...d5 in response, which White may or may not be happy about.
Or White can try to do without the move c3, taking advantage of the fact that Black's c6-knight can't currently come to a5 and swap the bishop off because the e5-pawn would fall.
With the move
8. h3, White eyes a transposition back to the main line with 8...d6 9.c3, while reserving the option of reacting to ...d5 by quickly developing the b1-knight to c3, hence the name Ambidextrous Variation.
8. a4 is a radical change of course and was Gary Kasparov's choice. White takes advantage of the fact that Black a) hasn't forced the move c3, and b) can't play ...c6 because the knight is needed on c6 to defend e5, and hatches a plan of ganging up on the adventurous Black b-pawn with a4 and Nc3, while incidentally giving the bishop a retreat square on a2.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5
column3:
Black's position is now reasonable. If White allows them, Black is now ready to take twice on d4 and so cement their extra pawn of material. Therefore White must reclaim the lost pawn now, or have nothing to show for it.
8. dxe5 is by far the main way to do this. This exposes an attack on d5, which Black defends with 8...Be6.
8. Nxe5 is playable but uncommon. Black exchanges off the knight that is currently obstructing his c-pawn. 8...Nxe5 9. dxe5 c6.
8. Re1 would grant Black equality.
8. c4 is the extraordinarily rare Harksen gambit, where White sacrifices their c-pawn for either 8...dxc4 9. Bc2 where the knight on e4 is undefended or 8...bxc4 9. Ba4 where White's bishop is back on the a4-e8 diagonal.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 f5 Nc3 fxe4 Nxe4 d5 Nxe5 dxe4 Nxc6 Qd5
column3: Both of White's developed pieces are threatened with capture, so 8. c4 is necessary to distract the Black queen.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 f5 Nc3 fxe4 Nxe4 d5 Nxe5 dxe4 Nxc6 Qg5
column3: White turns the tables on Black with 8. Qe2, defending the b5-bishop and attacking the e4-pawn. The discovered check isn't as exciting as it looks thanks to the possibility of ...c6 in response. There's nothing to be gained by the panicked retreat 8.Nd4+ c6 9.Bf1, for example.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4 Nc3 Nxe4
column3: Black accepts the gambit pawn, otherwise she will allow White to maintain a massive center. White follows her plan with 8. O-O

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Nxe4 Re1 d5 Bxd5 Qxd5
column3: Qxd5 recaptures the bishop. Now the only sensible response by White is Nc3, using the d1 to d5 pin and the e1 to e8 pin to fork the queen and double attack the knight.\nAs mentioned, the only move for White is 8. Nc3.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Na5 Bb5 c6 dxc6 bxc6
column3:
This is the main line of the Two Knights Defence. Black has sacrificed a pawn but in return has gained a lead in development, as well as a better central situation.
White's bishop is attacked. It may be moved, or the attacking pawn may be pinned instead.
8. Be2 is the old main line. White retreats the bishop to a square where it doesn't block any of white's pawns, but on the other hand, the white knight on g5 is vulnerable to being chased all around the board.
8. Bd3 is the modern main line. White blocks the d-pawn, but in return, gains the e4 square available for the knight to retreat, therefore this discourages 8...h6 because of 9. Ne4! in which White would gain an advantage.
8. Ba4? looks to be natural, but is in fact a blunder because of 8...h6 9. Nf3 e4!, in which white's knight either has to go back to g1, or move to e5, in which 10...Qd4 wins material.
8. Qf3 pins the c6 pawn to the rook on a8, and also attacks the c6 pawn for the second time. Black can in fact play 8...cxb5 sacrificing the exchange for a massive lead in development, but more often continues with 8...Be7 or 8...Rb8.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Ne7 Qg4 Kf8
column3:
Black moves the king to defend the weakness on g7.
When this variation started rising in popularity in the eighties, players with White used to play 8. Nf3, after which Black can put more pressure on White's queenside with 8...Qa5 9. Bd2 Qa4 10. Ra2, after which Black has an easier time trading off the light-squared bishops, since White's usual response a4 for trading the bishops on White's terms is no longer available.
Nowadays, moves like 8. a4 and 8. Bd2 are more popular, which dissuade Black's plan of trading the bishops. 8. a4 does this by occupying the a4 square in advance, and 8. Bd2 does this by rendering 8...Qa5 ineffective, since it no longer comes with tempo on the c3-pawn, allowing 9. a4 ⩲.
Another popular response is 8. h4, preparing an attack on Black's kingside and allowing for the rook on h1 to be brought into the attack faster through Rh3.
The variation is named after Vereslav Eingorn who started using it in 1983, employing it many times in the following years.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Ne7 Qg4 O-O
column3:
Although castling to the side where White wants to attack seems to be dangerous for Black, there are no
immediate mating threats - at least as long as White's queen is attacking Black's kingside on her own and without
support from other pieces.
That's why White usually decides to develop some additional pieces which may help with White's kingside attack. Typically this is done by playing 8. Nf3 or 8. Bd3, on rare occasions 8. h4 has also been tried. Note that 8. Bh6 is harmless for Black, who can defend against 9. Qxg7# by playing 8...Nf5 or 8...Ng6, in both cases White's dark-squared bishop must retreat and White wasted a tempo.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Ne7 Qg4 Qc7
column3:
Black lets White take the pawn on g7, but will break apart White's queenside in return. If White chooses to accept Black's pawn sacrifice, incredibly complex positions arise where general chess principles lose all meaning.
After 8. Qxg7, the main line, complications arise. The destruction of Black's kingside forces them to eventually castle long, where White has the open b-file to be used in an attack. Moreover, if all pieces are traded and an endgame arises, White will have good chances of promoting the passed h-pawn. Black will have to respond aggressively.
Less common is 8. Bd3, declining the pawn for now and preparing to castle short.
This variation was first played in 1945 between Vasily Panov and Viacheslav Ragozin. The game followed what is still considered to be the main line up to move 13, where Panov played 13. Be3. This can be attributed to the 7...cxd4 move order having been employed a decade prior already.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 e6 Bg5 dxc4 e4 b5 e5 h6 Bh4
column3: White retains the pin on Black's knight, threatening to take it with the pawn. Black must respond adequately with 8...g5, removing the bishop from the diagonal.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 e6 e3 Nbd7 Bd3 dxc4 Bxc4 b5 Bd3
column3: White returns the bishop to its original position, from where it supports the e4 pawn push. This is considered to be the main line.\nThe classical response by Black is 8...a6, protecting the b4-pawn in order to be able to free the light-squared bishop with c5 later. This does allow White to take control of the center with the immediate 9. e4, after which some very complicated positions can arise.\nA slightly more modern and nowadays more popular response is 8...Bb7, the Wade variation. This makes the immediate 9. e4 less desirable for White, who usually responds by castling kingside immediately.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 e3 e6 Bxc4 Bb4 O-O
column3:
White castles their king to safety to unpin the knight and to start preparing e4.
Black can now choose to either play 8...Nbd7 or 8...O-O. Play is very likely to transpose, but different deviations from the main line are possible depending on which move Black plays first. The main difference is that after 8...O-O, Black has many possibilities of fully preventing e4, while after 8...Nbd7 trying to do so is more dangerous for Black.
In both positions, White is likely to play Qe2, preparing e4. There is, however, another option.
It is not uncommon for White to play an early Nh4, chasing away the bishop. This option is most effective if White hasn't played 9. Qe2 yet, so that Qc2 can be played while gaining a tempo on the pawn.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 e6 f3 Bb4 e4
column3:
White takes over the centre, attacking Black's bishop and opening up an attack on the c4-pawn. Retreating the bishop would be a mistake, since this gives White the full centre without any compensation.
Sacrificing the knight with 8...Nxe4? doesn't work, since after 9. fxe4 Qh4+ White can move their king to safety on the kingside. If 9. fxe4 Bxe4 Black doesn't have any pressure on the c3-knight, so 10. Be3 keeps everything held.
Thus, 8...Bxe4! is the main move to not have a passive position. White doesn't have much better than 9. fxe4, after which 9...Nxe4 threatens 10...Nxc3 11. bxc3 Bxc3+ 12. Bd2 Qxd4 to pick up a fifth pawn for the piece. White has two options in this position.
10. Bd2 defends against ...Nxc3, but blocks the queen's view of the d4-pawn. 10...Qxd4 continues the variation and the following are only moves: 11. Nxe4 Qxe4+ 12. Qe2 (protecting the knight on e4) 12...Bxd2 13. Kxd2 Qd5+ and the king usually moves to the queenside with 14. Kc2. White will soon win back the c4-pawn and in the resulting position Black has three pawns for the piece. From this position, the game is generally decided by the endgame. Black has to prove that their three pawns are more valuable in this endgame than White's bishop, but the records show this position to generally be favourable for White.
White is not forced to take on this endgame. They can play 10. Qf3, defending c3 and forking the knight on e4 and the pawn on f7. Black's only move is 10...Qxd4 and after 11. Qxf7 Kd8 12. Bg5+ Nxg5 13. Qxg7 Black has nothing better than a series of checks with the queen after 13...Bxc3+ 14. bxc3 Qxc3+ leading to an eventual threefold repetition.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 Nbd7 Nxc4 Qc7 g3
column3: This move prepares to develop both bishops; the dark-squared bishop to f4 and the light-squared bishop to g2. This move doesn't deter Black from playing 8...e5 which has been prepared with Black's previous moves.

column1: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Be7 Bf4 O-O e3 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Qc2
column3: 8. Qc2\nWhite activates the queen, who points towards the black kingside. Black develops with 8...Nc6

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5 Nb3 Be6 f3
column3:
f3 might look like a slight inaccuracy. After all, never move the f-pawn right? As it turns out, this is by far the best move for white. f3 achieves multiple things at once:
Ng4, attempting to chop off the bishop, is now impossible.
e4 is now supported by a pawn instead of a piece (That might come under pressure in the future!)
If both sides castle on opposite sides, g4 and h4 are much easier to pull off.
In addition, the slight weakness created along the diagonal cannot be exploited by Black. The queen will take a lot of time to mobilize, and after Qh4+ g3 ends the attack right in its tracks. Like most of the English Attack, this move is directly taken from the Yugoslav Attack.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 b5 e5
column3: Moves : 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 b5 8.e5\nA logical move which wants to attack the Black knight. Indeed this knight seems to be immobilized by the White bishop.\n8...dxe5 (main line)

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 Qb6 Qd2
column3: Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 Qb6 8.Qd2\nWhite allows Black to take the pawn. Having played 7...Qb6, Black should take the pawn now with 8...Qxb2. If Black radically changes plans and does not take the pawn, White will simply castle queenside (9. 0-0-0), protecting the pawn, and the Black queen will be out of place on b6, it would prefer to be on c7 where it doesn't obstruct the b-pawn.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 O-O Qd2
column3: Qd2 is the most popular continuation. White prepares to castle queenside, but typically doesn't play Bh6 to exchange bishops. This opposite-castling game leads to sharp attacking positions where the two side pawns open the king's castle.\nOverwhelmingly popular (160 times more popular in the chess.com database than the second most popular) is 8...Nc6.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nb5 d6 c4 Nf6 N1c3 a6 Na3
column3:
White saves their knight with 8. Na3.
The position is looking cramped for Black. Those pawns on c4 and e4 prevent them from playing d5 and gaining more space. Meanwhile, Black's pawns on d6 and e6 prevent Black from developing their bishops very actively.
They have three typical continuations.
Black still has their bishops to develop, so option one is to develop their light-square bishop, in which case first Black must play 8...b6 to make room to fianchetto it.
Option two is to develop their dark-square bishop. Fianchettoing it is inconceivable of course because of how weak f6 will become. Since White induced them to play 5...d6, there is only one place left for it, so Black may as well play 8...Be7 and get it over with, then at least they can castle.
Option three is to discard both these options as too timid, throw caution at the wind, and kick open the Maroczy bind with 8...d5 anyway. This is an especially good continuation if it is 1985 and you are Garry Kasparov, after whom the audacious play, the Garry gambit, is named.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3
column3: With White preparing to strike in the centre with d4, Black's king typically vacates the premises with 8...O-O. The old-fashioned move is 8...Na5, which may transpose, but the loss of control over d4 may allow White to save a tempo by omitting h3.\n8...Bg4 is seen from time to time, discouraging an instant d4 by White. White will probably play d3 as a temporary measure, aiming to bring the queens knight to the kingside to evict the bishop in order to achieve d4.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 d4
column3:
White counts the number of pieces attacking d4, and the number of pieces defending it, and reckons that 8. d4 is a safe move.
However, 8...Nxd4 9. Nxd4 exd4 10. Qxd4?? and Black has 10...c5!. Wherever White's queen moves, Black follows up with 11...c4 and the bishop is trapped. This motif is called the Noah's Ark trap, because that's how old it is.
10. c3, treating the attack as a gambit, is occasionally played but White has insufficient compensation.
Leon Rosen tried this line against Mikhail Chigorin in Paris in 1900. Chigorin did not play the best move, 8...Nxd4. He continued 8...Bg5, pinning the knight and allowing White to secure the pawn with 9. c3.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4
column3:
Black's b5-pawn has come under attack, and its defence by the a6-pawn is only illusory as that pawn will be pinned along the a-file after axb5. Black must take other steps to defend it. Capturing on a4 would be an undesirable way out, because Bxa4 in response would renew the pressure on the c6-knight, and by extension the e5-pawn, that Black already went to the trouble of removing with 6...b5.
8...Bb7 defends the pawn indirectly by defending the a8-rook, thus cutting out the a-file pin, while also developing Black's last minor piece.
8...b4 removes the pawn from the danger square, closing the queenside and taking away the c3 square from White's b1-knight.
8...b4 has scored better in high-level games than 8...Bb7, so Black seems to benefit from retaining the option of developing the c8-bishop along the h3-c8 diagonal, and also from taking the Nc3 option away from White - a move with the side-effect of threatening the b5-pawn again, thus provoking Black into playing ...b4 anyway. As usual in the Closed Ruy Lopez, getting pieces off the back rank (which 8...Bb7 would achieve) is not either side's top priority, especially for Black who is slightly ahead in development. Now every pawn advance gives up squares along with gaining squares, and 8...b4 does give White the extra option of sending the b1-knight to c4 via d2, from whence it can hop across to its favourite square e3 and eventually f5 - but it has a perfectly good route to e3 already, via d2 and f1.
A sideline is 8...Rb8, which directly defends the pawn but at the cost of abandoning the a-file to White.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3
column3:
Black can now pull the trigger on the Marshall Gambit, sacrificing a pawn to quickly activate all her pieces while stripping the White kingside of defenders, with
8...d5
Alternatively,
8...d6
transposes back to the Closed Main Line (7...d6 8.c3 O-O). This move is actually more common than the Marshall Gambit, although it's the Marshall Gambit which makes 7...O-O into a significant alternative to 7...d6.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5 dxe5
column3:
White recovers the pawn and exposes an attack on d5. Black must drop everything and defend the d-pawn.
8...Be6 is the best way. This defends the pawn, develops, and stabilises the centre.
For the sake of completeness, the other ways to defend the pawn are 8...Ne7 and 8...d4. Absolutely no Brownie points for either of these moves:
8...Ne7 is the Zukertort variation. This defends the pawn but doesn't develop a new piece and is slow. White can give up the bishop pair and still have a commanding position.
8...d4? is horrible. It pulls the rug out from under the e4-knight while not particularly improving the pawns condition. 9. Re1 Nc5 10. Ng5! with the idea of Qf3, and even winning the bishop pair is not enough to keep Black in the game.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4 Nc3 Nxe4 O-O
column3: White castles her king. This unpins her knight to her king, causing the black knight on e4 to be hanging. Due to the open e-file creating complications should black retreat her knight, black generally exchanges on c3. While …Nxc3 is appealing to keep the bishop pair, it enters the rabbit hole.\nTherefore, Black should play …Bxc3, where after exchanging, there is no hanging piece, giving her time to play …d5

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Nxe4 Re1 d5 Bxd5 Qxd5 Nc3
column3: Nc3! uses the queen to queen pin as well as the rook to king pin to fork the Black queen and knight, which will fall the next turn. Black most commonly moves the queen to a5 or h5.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Na5 Bb5 c6 dxc6 bxc6 Be2
column3: White retreats the bishop to the natural square. It also partly protects the King side position.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Na5 Bb5 c6 dxc6 bxc6 Qf3
column3: Develops the queen and pins the c6 pawn, as ...cxb5 gives Qxa8.\nThis variation has become popular in light of the game Nigel Short vs Mark Hebden in which Short won convincingly. However, computer analysis has suggested that Black has full compensation for the pawn.\nBlack now faces the prospect of giving up a second pawn or the a8 Rook in order to maintain a development advantage.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Na5 d3 h6 Nf3 e4 Qe2
column3: Pins Black's pawn to Black's king, leaving it unable to capture White's vulnerable knight.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Nd4 c3 b5 Bf1 Nxd5 Ne4
column3: 8. Ne4. A testing move.\nNow Black's Knight on d4 is at risk while the White Knight aids to the defence of the King side.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxf7 Kxf7 Qf3 Ke6 Nc3
column3: Attacking the central knight. Black must reply by moving the c6-knight to b4 (defending d5 with tempo and preparing c6).\n8. ... Ne7?? is a huge mistake that lets white open the center with 9. d4! and strengthen the attack on the black king.\nAfter 8. ... Nd4??, instead, 9. Bxd5+ followed by 10. Qd1 let white get back the piece and defend the c2 pawn. Black has survived the attack but is a pawn down with a very weak e pawn.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Ne7 Qg4 Qc7 Bd3
column3:
White does not go for the craziness that arises from accepting the poisoned pawn but develops the kingside instead.
While White has a much easier time castling kingside, this may not be beneficial, especially when Black's kingside is opened up or far-advanced like in Carlsen - Rapport, 2024.
Black's main responses involve trying to force White's pieces onto "bad" squares.
8...c4 questions the bishop's placement immediately, forcing it back to e2 (9. Bf1 would be a waste of time). After this, Black has two options:
9...Qa5 puts more pressure on the queenside and forces White's dark-squared bishop to d2. This queen move is very thematic for the Winawer and is the central point of the Portisch Hook variation. Maneuvers for both sides can be observed in Shankland - Mishra, 2023.
Black can also go for the immediate 9...Nf5, waiting to see what White does and potentially transposing back to 9...Qa5 lines. In both lines, Black will be able to keep their kingside intact thanks to the knight jumping to f5 to defend the g-pawn.
8...cxd4 is more aggressive, often leading to more poisoned-pawn-esque positions. Black leaves White's bishop on d3 and allows White to eventually take on g7 because this pawn can no longer be defended with Nf5. 8...cxd4 requires White to respond with 9. Ne2. Theory continues 9...dxc3 10. Qxg7 Rg8 11. Qxh7 Qxe5 ∞ with a very double edged position: White's king is stuck in the centre, but White has good prospects in an endgame thanks to the outside passed h-pawn.
8...Qa5 simply transposes into the 8...c4 lines after 9. Bd2 c4 10. Be2.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Ne7 Qg4 Qc7 Qxg7
column3: White calls Black's bluff and takes the g7 pawn.\nBlack doesn't have anything better than 8...Rg8. The only alternative 8...Rf8? would be too passive.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 e6 Bg5 dxc4 e4 b5 e5 h6 Bh4 g5
column3: Black blocks the vision of White's dark-squared bishop in order to save the knight. It seems that White's attack is finally over but 9. Nxg5 continues the attack, temporarily sacrificing the knight for two pawns to win it back later.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 e6 e3 Nbd7 Bd3 dxc4 Bxc4 b5 Bd3 a6
column3:
Black protects the b-pawn so they can play 9...c5 without blundering a pawn.
Foreseeing this plan, White should play actively and take over the center with 9. e4, preparing to open up the center with either 10. d5 or 10. e5 and opening up the dark-squared bishop.
Less provocative setups have been tried as well. At the amateur level 9. O-O is very popular, but this poses no problems for players with the black pieces at all, since they score quite well in this line.
Another move that is played often is 9. a4. White does better than after 9. O-O, but has lost quite a bit of initiative.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 e3 e6 Bxc4 Bb4 O-O O-O
column3: Black quickly castles their king to safety. This gives Black the option of playing 9...Bg6, which prevents 10. e4 and results in positions where White doesn't get as much central control.\nWhite's main option is still 9. Qe2, threatening to play 10. e4.\nWhite can also opt for 9. Nh4, transposing into the Bled attack.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 Nbd7 Nxc4 Qc7 g3 e5
column3:
Black finally pushes the e pawn forward, releasing the dark-squared bishop and fighting for the center.
If White ignores the pawn and prepares to castle with 9. Bg2, Black can start building pressure with 9...Rd8, aiming at White's queen, and 10...Be6 pressuring the knight (if 9...O-O-O then 10. a5! followed by 11. Qa4 starts a nasty attack on the queenside).
Therefore, White's best option is 9. dxe5, exchanging pawns in the center.
The Carlsbad variation is likely named after the tournament with the move's first appearance, that being the Karlsbad tournament from 1929. It was featured in a game between Capablanca and Vidmar.

column1: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Be7 Bf4 O-O e3 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Qc2 Nc6

column3:
8...Ne7
We have reached the Mar del Plata variation, the quintessential line of the King’s Indian Defense.
The center is locked for the moment. Black’s plan is to launch a furious kingside assault aimed to crash through White's kingside and have a chat with the white king. This is achieved with the help of a pawn storm starting with ...f5. Black would also try to hold together their queenside to slow down White’s potential counterattacks and hope their attack lands faster.
In contrast, White’s plans are to combine a queenside counterattack with smart manoeuvring and defense on the kingside. White has to be very precise here, but if they manage to survive Black’s attack, White’s space advantage in the center and queenside, and material advantage given Black will likely have to sacrifice material to keep their kingside initiative going, will give them the edge.
Black usually plays ...Nd7, ...Ne8 or ...Nh5 depending on the situation. This frees up the pawn break with ...f7-f5, kickstarting the kingside attack. Black can continue this pawn storm with ...f5-f4 (usually in response to f2-f3 by White), ...g6-g5 and ...h7-h5.
Especially if White manages to play cxd6, the c7 and d6 squares are major vulnerabilities in Black’s position, and can be exploited with Nb5. Thus, Black reorganises their pieces on the kingside to deal with this, while simultaneously helping their kingside effort. Firstly, Black routes the e7 knight to g6, where it supports the kingside attack, can route to e8 to defend c7 and d6 if needed, and clears the 7th rank. Next, Black plays Gilgoric’s famous rook lift, ...Rf7. This not only helps defend c7, but also frees up f8 for the next maneuver, ...Bf8, adding a defending to d6. Black may also want to route their other knight back to f6, helping the kingside attack, and frees up the c8 bishop.
It may not be obvious to you, but Black’s light-squared bishop standing there undeveloped on c8 is a crucial part of Black's kingside attack. If the time is right, this bishop could sacrifice itself on g4 or h3 to burst open White's kingside.
White has 3 main setups in the Mar del Plata variation.
9. Ne1, the Classical System used to be White’s main line in the Mar del Plata variation. Given that the knight on f3 won’t do much and can even be a target for attack, White reroutes the knight to d3. This also allows White to play f2-f3, shoring up White’s kingside pawn chain. By freeing the f2 square, it allows White to develop the bishop to e3 and retreat it to f2 upon being attacked by ...f5-f4. The bishop on the g1-a7 diagonal has nice future prospects, due to this diagonal being free of pawns.
9. b4, is the fearsome Bayonet Attack. Instead of trying to weather Black’s kingside storm, White launches a fierce counterattack on the queenside, fighting fire with fire. This line is considered to be White’s most challenging variation against the King’s Indian Defense as a whole, gaining this reputation after Kramnik used it with success against Kasparov. Black will need to play very precisely to retain chances here.
9. Nd2, the Modern System is no longer popular after the discovery of the Bayonet Attack, but is still played occasionally. White plans to play b2-b4, c4-c5, then install a monstrous knight on c4.

Today the line is just as messy as it was in its heyday in the 1970s, but is now considered to be equal with best play. Today there have been lines analyzed up to twenty or thirty moves in depth, such as this one, the main one.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 O-O Qd2 Nc6
column3:
Both sides have now sufficiently developed and white faces a major dilemma for their next move:
- 9. Bc4 was originally the most popular and critical line. White controls d5 as much as possible, trying to restrict all central counterplay from white. The mainline then follows 9...Bd7 10. 0-0-0 Rc8 11. Bb3 and both sides go on an all out attack on each other's king.
- 9. 0-0-0 was seen until recently a refuted line that allowed black to immediately equalize and avoid the massive pawn storm coming at them. With the advent of engines it was revealed that white actually maintains a larger, positional advantage. This led to a theory war with many top players trying to find deep ideas for each color up until the endgame.
- 9. g4 is a hyper aggressive variation that has the very simple and easy idea of punching black in the face as soon as possible by immediately going on the offensive. This variation is known for being extremely dangerous to both sides, but engine analysis has shown that black has sufficient counterplay in the center to survive the attack easily.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nb5 d6 c4 Nf6 N1c3 a6 Na3 d5
column3:
Black challenges White in the centre to open up the position.
White has four attackers to Black's three defenders. However, after 9. cxd5 exd5 10. exd5, Black intends to play 10...Nb4, bringing another attacker.
The Garry gambit was first played by Garry Kasparov in two games of the 1985 World Championship match with Anatoly Karpov (see sample game).
After the discovery of the continuation 12. Be3 Bxe3 13. Qa4+! (see below) this fell out of favour for Black.
The sixteenth game of the World Championship match.
1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nc6 5. Nb5 d6 6. c4 Nf6 7. N1c3 a6 8. Na3 d5
Kasparov plays the "Garry gambit".
9. cxd5 exd5 10. exd5 Nb4
This position had already been reached in their twelfth game of the match. In that game, Karpov (playing White) continued 11. Bc4, a natural move to defend the pawn, and continued cautiously before having to settle for a draw: 11...Bg4 (compelling White's bishop to retreat) 12. Be2 Bxe2 13. Qxe2+ Qe7 14. Be3 Nbxd5 (Black recovers the pawn) 15. Nc2 Nxe3 16. Nxe3 Qe6 17. O-O Bc5 18. Rfe1 O-O ½-½.
11. Be2
This time White intends to control d5 with a Be2-Bf3 manoeuvre.
11...Bc5
Rather than take back the pawn, Black leaves it and focuses on development instead. They can quickly capitalise on good, active squares for their pieces, while White's knight on a3 is passive.
Kasparov analysed 11...Nbxd5 12. O-O Be7 13. Nxd5 Nxd5 14. Bf3 (attacking knight) Be6 (defending knight) 15. Nc2! as better for White. The c2 knight threatens to come to d4, where it can take bishop on e6 that is tied down to protect the knight. Black therefore avoids taking the pawn because of the difficulty in defending the knight on the d5 square.
12. O-O
When Karpov faced this line again in 1986, he played the improvement 12. Be3 Bxe3 13. Qa4+! forking the now-undefended knight on b4.
12...O-O 13. Bf3 Bf5
Black locks out the a3 knight from play. It now cannot go to c2, and Nc4 allows Bd3, forking the knight and the rook. (In fact, modern engines are happy with the transformation 14. Nc4 Bd3 15. Ne3 Bxf1 16. Kxf1 for White: willing to sacrifice the exchange to eliminate Black's active bishop and revive the prospects of White's knight).
14. Bg5 Re8 15. Qd2 b5 16. Rad1 Nd3
Black's knight takes over a superb outpost and dominates White's position. Black threatens b3, forking the knights.
17. Nab1 h6 18. Bh4 b4 19. Na4 Bd6
White's position is close to paralysis: Black's monstrous knight is preventing White from bringing their rooks into the game, White's knights have been pushed to the rim with nowhere to go, and now Black threatens to trap White's queen with Rc8 and Bf4.
20. Bg3
Forced, to prevent White's queen becoming trapped.
20...Rc8
Black had to discard two alternatives:
20...Ne4 21. Bxe4 Bxe4, winning the bishop pair and weakening White's d5 pawn. Seirawan's analysis picks out the danger of 22. Qe3 as a continuation, allowing White to untangle their position by playing Qb6 to trade queens (though the engine likes this for Black. One continuation is 22...Bf5 23. Qb6 Bxg3 24. Qxd8 Bxh2+ 25. Kxh2 Raxd8∓).
20...Bxg3 21. hxg3 Qa5 22. b3 Rad8 23. Na3 (the b3 pawn is pinned to Black's queen) Nxd5 and Black wins the d5 pawn, then 24. Nc4 Qb5 25. Bxd5 Rxd5 26. Ne3 Rdd8 27. Nxf5 Qxf5. Kasparov believed he had more chance to play for advantage by avoiding the trades and "tightening the screws on the position [asking] White how he intends to solve his problems."
Black takes the open c-file and control of even more of White's space.
21. b3
To allow Nb2: White hopes to trade off Black's monstrous knight.
21...g5 22. Bxd6 Qxd6 23. g3 Nd7 24. Bg2 Qf6
White can't get in Nb2 now. Their a4 knight is so out of play that they are practically down a piece; their b1 knight is no better.
25. a3 a5 26. axb4 axb4 27. Qa2
White is desperate to untangle their position and get some piece activity. Unable to shift Black's b pawn, White moves the queen to make room for Nd2 instead.
27...Bg6
Black can meet Nd2 with Re2!, pinning the knight to White's queen. However, if say 27...h5 28. Nd2 Re2, White has the defensive resource Bf2. By moving their bishop back, Black allows their queen to control f2 and 28. Nd2 Re2 29. Bf3 Rxd2 30. Qxd2 Qxf3-+ wins two pieces for a rook.
28. d6 g4 29. Qd2 Kg7 30. f3 Qxd6 31. fxg4 Qd4+ 32. Kh1 Nf6 33. Rf4 Ne4 34. Qxd3 Nf2+ 35. Rxf2 Bxd3 36. Rfd2 Qe3 37. Rxd3 Rc1 38. Nb2 Qf2 39. Nd2 Rxd1+ 40. Nxd1 Re1+
Black has mate in 2 (41. Nf1 Rxf1+ 42. Bxf1 Qxf1#). White resigns.

column3: 9. Bd3 is almost always played. Black has spent numerous tempos on this bishop, and since white usually aims to castle queenside, it makes sense to remove the light-squared bishop.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O
column3: White's most consistent move is 9. d4 freeing the queenside minor pieces and contesting the centre, however, it walks into 9...Bg4 after which the conventional wisdom is that Black has nothing to worry about. For this reason the d4 push is almost always prepared with 9. h3. A few masters have recently attempted to prove that 9. d4 is possible.\nWhite may be fed up with all these preparatory moves and play 9. d3 allowing the safe development of the queenside, but this gives Black complete freedom, claims less space than d4 and limits the scope of the light-squared bishop. The successful chess player must have patience!

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5
column3:
Black is attacking e4 twice and in general threatening to overrun the centre of the board. White has no better option than to accept the proffered pawn with
9. exd5
followed by capturing twice on e5. Skip ahead to the end of that forcing variation if you like: 9. exd5 Nxd5 10. Nxe5 Nxe5 11. Rxe5.
However, White can also decline the gambit with 9.d4.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5 dxe5 Be6
column3:
Now that White's light-squared bishop can no longer move to d5, it is immobilised and liable to be exchanged off by a sneaky ...Na5 or ...Nc5. In the Ruy Lopez, White will typically go to some length to avoid this exchange, hence the classical move 9. c3. The modern alternative move order begins 9. Nbd2.
9. c3 is the traditional move. In the Ruy Lopez, White will typically go to some lengths to avoid trading this bishop for a knight. This prepares to answer 9...Nc5 with 10. Bc2.
Since 9...Nc5 doesn't get Black anywhere now, the main moves are 9...Be7 and 9...Bc5. After 9...Be7, as White's knight can't make it to c3, they usually play Nbd2 intending Bc2 and Nb3. 9...Be7 10. Nbd2 O-O 11. Bc2 f5 12. Nb3 and the two move orders, 9. c3 and 9. Nbd2, have converged. After 9...Bc5, this increases pressure on f2: 10. Nbd2, the St. Petersburg variation, 10...O-O 11. Bc2 Nxf2 12. Rxf2 f6. 10. Qd3, the Motzko attack, supports 11. Bd3 to relieve pressure on f2.
9. Nbd2, the Bernstein variation, has taken over in popularity in recent years. White can live without the light-square bishop in this particular line, as they have a kingside pawn majority to work with, so long as they can recapture on b3 with the knight and avoid doubling their pawns. In fact, 9...Nc5 10. c3 Nxb3 11. Nxb3 would free White's position enormously. The knight on b3 has better prospects than either a bishop on b3 or a knight on d2.
In addition, the 9. Nbd2 move order avoids the complications following 9...Bc5, as 10. Nxe4 ends the double attack on f2. After some exchanges, White's other knight can capture on e4 or e6, hitting the loose bishop.
9. Be3 also discourages ...Bc5, but no more effectively than Nbd2, and unlike Nbd2 it does not develop a piece to what is clearly its best square. The appeal of this order is that White gets to answer 9...Nc5 with 10. Nbd2 without impeding the development of their bishop. However, 10...d4 and the bishop must move again.
9. Qe2 is the Howell attack. First, this vacates d1 for the rook, where it will pin black's d-pawn. 9...Be7 10. Rd1 O-O 11. c4! bxc4 12. Bxc4 and the d-pawn is pinned. Secondly, it allows White to answer ...Bc5 with Be3 and trade the bishops, recapturing without doubling pawns. 12...Bc5 13. Be3 Bxe3 14. Qxe3=.
This rearrangement is on the slow side  given that Black is only a couple of moves away from completing their development, and too often White's play on the d-file consists of trying to stop Black's passed d-pawn from charging down it.
9. a4 is apparently played. Compared to the Worrall attack, 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 a6 4. Ba4 Nf6 5. O-O Be7 6. Qe2, where the idea of a4 is to provoke b4 (6...b5 7. Bb3 d6 8. a4 b4? where 9. Qc4! is ruinous, a double attack on c6 and f7), here eliciting ...b4 does not create a weakness on c4 so in that sense 9. a4 is erring a little on the pointless side. Save it for later, maybe.

For this reason, it has gained a reputation for being an unexciting opening which has almost always led to draws in games between grandmasters. However, some players have argued that White holds an imbalance with a kingside majority while Black's bishop pair can dominate the board.\nGM Vladimir Kramnik was the one who popularized the position among chess players like Magnus Carlsen and Viswanathan Anand.

column3: Black saves their rook and threatens White's queen.\nWhite's main and only good move is 9. Qxh7. Not only does White win a pawn, their queen is positioned to come back to d3 to defend White's queenside when needed. Eliminating Black's h-pawn also turns White's h-pawn into a passed pawn, providing an important advantage when entering an endgame.

column3: White strikes in the center, opening up the dark-squared bishop in the process.\nBlack's main move is 9...c5, looking to break up White's center immediately. This move is played in the vast majority of games, and is Black's best option to open up the light-squared bishop and fight for an advantage.\nA very rare sideline is 9...b4, the Pirc variation. This is the only other move (according to chess engines) that doesn't give White a winning advantage, since it gains a tempo on White's knight.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 e3 e6 Bxc4 Bb4 O-O O-O Qe2
column3:
White is threatening to play 10. e4 with a tempo on the bishop. If Black allows this, they will have to fend off White's king-side attack, which comes in very quickly.
9...Nbd7 is considered to be the main line. Black allows White to play e4 and hopes to fend off White's attack. The knight can serve as a potential defender by repositioning to f8.
Black has many options for preventing e4. The most popular being 9...Bg6.
After 9...Bg6 Black prevents e4 tactically. By retreating the bishop, 10. e4? is no longer played with tempo and in response Black plays 10...Bxc3! 11. bxc3 Nxe4 ∓ and White doesn't have the option of preventing Black from castling with Ba3 because Black is already castled. Because e4 isn't made possible, White generally chooses to try and capture the bishop with 10. Ne5.
A more direct way to prevent e4 is by occupying the square with a piece instead: 9...Ne4  blocks White's pawn and initiates a trade of pieces: 10. Bd3 and 10. Nxe4 are common. Black does however need to be prepared for the rare 10. g4! the Sämisch variation, where White is able to quickly storm Black's king with pawns.
Another way for Black to achieve this goal is by 9...Bg4, pinning and potentially capturing the f3 knight which is protecting d4. If White continues with their plan they will quickly find themselves down a pawn after 10. e4? Bxf3 11. gxf3 Qxd4 ⩱.

column3: 9. a3\nThis move is important to control the b4 square and support b2-b4. Black is forced to play 9...Qa5, which prevents b4 by pinning the a3 pawn to the rook and pins the c3 knight to the king. This also supports ...Nb4.

column3: The most popular move. After 9.Rb1 White chases away the Black queen and assumes control of the b-file. After the queen escapes to a3 (only move), White will have several options.
