column3: Bc4 develops the bishop to a good square, pinning the f7 pawn and aiming at the Black king and kingside to attack. On the next move White will castle queenside and a fierce attack is on!

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7 h5 Bh7 Bd3
column3: Black's almost invariable response of 9...Bxd3 is almost forced, although 9...Ngf6 and even 9...e6 have both been attempted, without much success.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O h3
column3:
The position in the Ruy Lopez after 9. h3 is one of the most strategically interesting in the whole of opening theory. Black's reasonable options at this point run to double figures, which for a position nine moves into the game is almost unique.
9...Na5 is the old main line, the Chigorin Variation. Black hunts down White's light-squared bishop and frees her c-pawn. The knight may end up back on c6, on c5 via b7, or on c4, depending on developments elsewhere.
9...Nb8, the Breyer Variation, is the other traditional move. With White taking her time developing her queenside, Black reckons she can spare two moves to redeploy the knight on d7 out of the way of the bishop which will appear on b7. It is a little more committal than the Chigorin and appeals to defensive-minded players.
9...Bb7, the Flohr, is the current red-hot theoretical battleground. The bishop eyes up the e4 pawn and the knight reserves its options.
9...h6 is the Smyslov Variation. The Zaitsev is considered an improvement on the Smyslov; in the Smyslov the bishop will usually go to b7, but in the Zaitsev Black can usually manage without ...h6.
9...Nd7 on the plus side enables an f5 advance and controls g5, and on the minus side clogs up the queenside and removes a defender from the king.
9...Be6 is another way to challenge the b3-bishop, usually leading to an exchange of bishops and a boring position in which White has a little more activity.
9...Re8 will transpose to the Zaitsev unless both players are desperate for a draw by repetition.
9...a5 is a quirky attempt to force matters on the queenside. White will probably meet it with a central charge.
9...Bd7 and 9...Qd7 are both at least semi-useful, and even 9...d5 doesn't lose on the spot - although players interested in getting their d-pawn to d5 should look at the Marshall Gambit on move 7.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5
column3: Black usually recaptures with 9...Nxd5, but the aggressive Steiner variation, 9...e4, has given Black surprising success at the amateur level.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5 dxe5 Be6 c3
column3:
9. c3 makes an escape square for White's bishop, so that ...Na5 or ...Nc5 no longer threatens to trade it off.
Next for Black is to develop their final minor piece and make way for castling, 9...Bc5 or 9...Be7.
9...Bc5 increases the pressure on f2. White plays 10. Nbd2 O-O 11. Bc2, the St. Petersburg variation, a threat to take twice on e4, removing Black's difficult advanced knight and winning the pawn. The old move is 11...f5, to defend the knight, but better is the surprising Dilworth variation, 11...Nxf2! 12. Rxf2 Bxf2+ 13. Kxf2 f6. Usually the trade of two minors for a rook and pawn is a bad deal, but here it works out and Black has a strong initiative with the f-file about to open.
9...Be7 is the classical defence, a more conservative developing move intending 10. Nbd2 O-O 11. Bc2 f5. Another line is 10...Nc5 11. Bc2 d4 12. Nb3, whereby Black can answer 9. c3 and 9. Nbd2, the Bronstein variation, in the same way.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5 dxe5 Be6 Nbd2
column3:
White develops their knight to d2.
This is the main alternative to 9. c3. After 9. c3, White can meet 9...Nc5 with 10 Bc2 and keep the bishop pair. Instead, 9. Nbd2 is an offer to trade bishop for knight. White allows 9...Nc5 10. c3 Nxb3!? as they can recapture 11. Nxb3 and avoid doubling their pawns.
However, on d2, White's knight obstructs the development of their bishop, so if Black doesn't take on b3, White will have to spend time untangling their position. Most common today is 9...Nc5 10. c3 Be7 (Black does not wish to trade and help White to improve their knight) 11. Bc2 (intending 12. Nb3), and the game might continue 11...d4 12. Nb3 dxc3 13. Nxc5 Bxc5 14. Be4 (attacking c6, which is pinned to a8) Qd7⩲.
10...d4 is an alternative. ...d4, before White has had chance to play Bc2, offers to trade the light-square bishops:
The old line goes 11. cxd4 Nxd4 12. Nxd4 Qxd4 13. Bxe6 Nxe6 14. Qf3 Rd8. More common nowadays is 11. Bxe6 Nxe6 12. cxd4 Ncxd4= for an even game.
11. Ng5!?, the Karpov gambit, was introduced in the World Championship Match in 1978. One idea behind the knight sacrifice is to allow White's queen to come to f3 and increase pressure on Black's weak long diagonal, 11...Qxg5 12. Qf3 Kd7?! (an attempt to defend the knight on c6) 13. Bd5!±. 12...Bd7 to defend the knight allows 13. Bxf7+!. The best move for Black is 12...O-O-O 13. Bxe6+ fxe6 14. Qxc6 Qxe5, allowing White to recover the knight.
9...Be7 is the main side line: seeing that hunting down the bishop is now less appetising, Black would simply like to castle and play f5. White still would like to play the c3, Bc2, Nb3 manoeuvre to straighten out their queenside.
If 9...Bc5, which increases pressure on f2 and is the main move after 9. c3, White can trade off the knight 10. Nxe4 dxe4 11. Ng5 (not a gambit this time!) Qxd1 12. Rxd1 Bxb3 13. axb3⩲.
Ossip Bernstein played this line against Siegbert Tarrasch in 1914.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Na5 Bb5 c6 dxc6 bxc6 Be2 h6 Nh3
column3: Steinitz Variation\nBobby Fischer revived this in the 1960s and Nigel Short in the 1990's.\nIt has an equally good reputation as the main line move 9 Nf3.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Ne7 Qg4 Qc7 Qxg7 Rg8 Qxh7
column3: White's queen steps out of the way of the rook and takes a pawn along the way.\nHaving given up their kingside, Black should keep playing actively and accurately to capitalize off of the fact that White has spent the past three moves moving their queen. 9...cxd4! is the best way to achieve this. Black regains one of their lost pawns and threatens 10...Qxc3+, which would pick up the rook. This also removes the only defender of the e5-pawn, making 10...Qxe5+ possible too.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 e6 e3 Nbd7 Bd3 dxc4 Bxc4 b5 Bd3 a6 e4 c5
column3:
Black strikes back at White's center, opening up the light-squared bishop.
This is the main branching point of the mainline Meran, since White has to choose between one of two pawn breaks: e5 and d5.
10. e5 is the Old variation.
10. d5 is Reynold's variation.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 Nbd7 Nxc4 Qc7 g3 e5 dxe5 Nxe5
column3: The central pawns have been exchanged. White can, and should, play 10. Bf4, developing the bishop and pinning the knight on e5. This also justifies White's previous move 8. g3.\nWhite's knight on c4 is hanging, so there isn't many alternatives. 10. Nxe5? doesn't develop any of White's pieces and allows Black to quickly catch up in development.

column1: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Be7 Bf4 O-O e3 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Qc2 Nc6 a3 Qa5
column3:
9...Qa5
This move is forced, pinning the a3 pawn to the rook, preventing b2-b4 and supporting ...Nb4 ideas. White has a sideline and 2 mainline moves.
10. Nd2 is the sideline, avoiding the complications of the mainlines. As Nb3 is threatened, black responds with ...Be7.
The mainlines 10. Rd1 and 10. O-O-O are not for the faint of heart, as they lead to wild, extremely complicated positions.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 b5 e5 dxe5 fxe5 Qc7
column3: Moves : 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6. Bg5 e6 7. f4 b5 8. e5 dxe5 9. fxe5 Qc7.\nNow White seems to gain space and Black seems to be undeveloped. But the following moves will show that its not so evident.\n10. exf6 (main line)

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 Qb6 Qd2 Qxb2 Rb1 Qa3
column3: This is the only move for Black's queen, and so should be self explanatory. Another move, 9...Nxe4? drops a piece not to 10.Nxe4?? Qxb1+ and Black is winning, but 10.Rxb2 Nxd2 11.Kxd2 and White is winning.\nHere White has a few choices. The most popular is 10.f5, applying direct pressure to e6. Then Black usually plays 10...Nc6 11.fxe6 fxe6 12.Nxc6 bxc6 13.e5 dxe5 14.Bxf6 gxf6 15.Ne4, when Black's best is 15...Qxa2 (or 15...Be7 16.Be2 h5 17.Rf1!, with a strong attack).\nWhite's other choices are 10.e5 and 10.Bxf6.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 O-O Qd2 Nc6 Bc4 Bd7
column3: Bd7 develops the bishop to its only good square at the moment. This  move also has a second purpose: to free the c8 square for the rook. In the Open Sicilians, Black gets a half open c-file in exchange for White's half-open d-file, and Bd7/Rc8 is a good way to take advantage of it. Rc8 also threatens White's c4-bishop, forcing it to move out of danger with most commonly Bb3.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7 h5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3
column3: Taking with the queen is of course the only response, to prevent the doubled, isolated pawns.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O h3 Bb7
column3: This is the main theoretical battleground in the Ruy Lopez today. Black's bishop aims at the White e-pawn, which will be ganged up on through moves like ...Re8 and ...Bf8, followed by taking on d4 to maximize the pressure. Meanwhile Black maintains maximum flexibility for the queen's knight: it may go to the traditional square a5, or to b4 once the c-pawn captures on d4. Karpov favored this line in his glory days of the '70s and '80s. Now it has greatly decreased in popularity in the last twenty years, but still leads to very complex, difficult positions.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O h3 Na5
column3: This is the old main line. Black chases white's bishop from the effective a2-g8 diagonal. Not only that, black opens up the c-pawn to expand on the queen side. Usually, after 10. Bc2 and 10…c5, if allowed, black will play 11…Nc6 and black ends up with a space advantage on the queen side.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 e4
column3: This aggressive move, attacking the Nf3, is rarely seen in high-level master play, however at amateur levels, the Steiner variation has given Black surprising success.\n10. dxc6 is the best and most popular move, trading knights. However, this scores very poorly for White due to plenty of tricks that may arise after 10...exf3 11. Qxf3?! Bg4.\n10. Ng5!? is scores well at club level, however after 10...Na5! Black is objectively better as they are threatening to receive the bishop pair.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Na5 Bb5 c6 dxc6 bxc6 Be2 h6 Nf3 e4
column3: With the pawn under a attack, challenging the White Knight again is an obviously useful move here, as it gains a tempo.

column1: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Ne7 Qg4 Qc7 Qxg7 Rg8 Qxh7 cxd4
column3:
Black captures the d4-pawn, opening up the queen and removing the defender of the e5-pawn.
It might not be immediately clear how White should respond. 10. cxd4?? defends e5, but blunders 10...Qc3+ 11. Bd2 Qxa1+ -+. Defending just c3 with 10. Bd2? or 10. Bb2? fails due to 10...Qxe5+, taking the e5-pawn with check or 10...dxc3 gaining a tempo on the bishop.
Therefore, White's best move by far is 10. Ne2. This protects c3 and prevents 10...Qxe5 with 11. cxd4, regaining the pawn with tempo. This move does have one downside: the knight is in the way of the light-squared bishop, so it doesn't bring White any closer to castling.
Also possible is 10. Qd3. White gives up the central pawns and offers a queen trade after 10...Qxe5+ 11. Ne2 dxc3 12. Qxc3. Black's best option is to take, after which the game has entered a queenless middlegame where White has a very dangerous passed pawn on the h-file.
10. Kd1 was common, but hasn't been played more than twice a year since 1999.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 e6 Bg5 dxc4 e4 b5 e5 h6 Bh4 g5 Nxg5 hxg5 Bxg5
column3: White recaptures the pawn, reestablishing the pin on the knight. Black can't avoid White gaining his piece back and should continue development. 10...Nbd7 is the usual reply, representing the starting point of the Botvinnik variation.\n10...Be7 is another option, although it leads to many trades resulting in a very simplified position, which usually isn't the goal of players going into the Botvinnik.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 Nbd7 Nxc4 Qc7 g3 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Bf4
column3: This move pins the knight on e5 to the black queen, which is its only defender at the moment. Moving the knight isn't an option, so the only move to add another defender is 10...Nfd7.\n10...Bd6?? fails to defend the knight because it loses a piece. The d6 square is attacked by both the c4 knight and the queen on d1 and only defended by Black's queen on c7.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 O-O Qd2 Nc6 Bc4 Bd7 O-O-O
column3: White castles queenside. Black should aim at White's king with Rc8 or Qa5 next, but other moves such as Ne5 are possible. Both sides often use their pawns on a6 and b6 (Black) or g2 and h2 (White) to open lines on the side they are attacking.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7 h5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3
column3: Previously, all three main responses (...Ngf6, ...e6, ...Qc7) were thought to be equivalent, and often transposed to the same position with black castling queenside. Later development saw Black look at castling kingside, but for a while this fell out of favour as White found he could move his knight to e4 or e2, and advance g4, without needing to prepare Rg1. This extra tempo seems to threaten this line as a viable alternative for black, as white can win the race between the white kingside and black queenside attacks. More recent theory, however, has seen Black resurrect ...e6, quite often not castling at all, while the other alternatives remain out of favour.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5
column3: Black takes the opportunity to swap off White's useful central knight and instead draw the e1-rook out to a vulnerable square on the fifth rank, with10...Nxe5.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Na5 Bb5 c6 dxc6 bxc6 Be2 h6 Nf3 e4 Ne5
column3: The Knights moves to the center of the board, here it can easily be attacked again by Black, but White now has the opportunity to defend it with d4 or f4 or even consider retreating the Knight to g4 or c4.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Na5 d3 h6 Nf3 e4 Qe2 Nxc4 dxc4 Bc5 Nfd2
column3: Retreats the vulnerable knight to avoid capture after Black escapes the pin by castling.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 e6 Bg5 dxc4 e4 b5 e5 h6 Bh4 g5 Nxg5 hxg5 Bxg5 Nbd7
column3:
Black defends the knight on f6 again to prevent 11. Bxf6 forking the queen and the rook.
This is the first big branching point in the Botvinnik variation. White has two main options.
11. g3, the Lilienthal variation, delays capturing the knight on f6 and prepares to fianchetto White's light-squared bishop.
11. exf6 takes the hanging knight immediately. While it often transposes back into the Lilienthal, it gives Black more options to deviate from the Lilienthal.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 Nbd7 Nxc4 Qc7 g3 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Bf4 Nfd7
column3: This move defends the pinned knight. White no longer has any moves to increase the pressure on the e5 knight, so play usually continues by developing the light-squared bishop with 11. Bg2.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 O-O Qd2 Nc6 Bc4 Bd7 O-O-O Rc8
column3: Black takes advantage of the half-open c-file they received in the Open Sicilian, and aims at the hanging c4-bishop. As Nxd4 Qxd4 Ng4! takes advantage of the overworked White queen and Black is attacking both bishops at once, White typically moves the bishop to safety with Bb3, keeping an eye on the Black king.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7 h5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6
column3: 11. Bf4 is the most challenging response  when faced with modern Black theory where Black does not castle queenside. In earlier theory, when Black planned to castle queenside, Bd2 was almost equivalent. The other alternatives offer little for White.

column1: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nxe4 Qh5 Nd6 Bb3 Nc6 Nb5 g6 Qf3 f5 Qd5 Qe7 Nxc7 Kd8 Nxa8 b6
column3: The players have reached the base position of the Frankenstein-Dracula opening. Such variant owes its name to Tim Harding, a chess author that, in his 1973 book "Bishop’s Opening", commented that, because of its extreme sharpness, it would have been appropriate for a duel between the two literary monsters. Harding then explicitly introduced the name "Frankenstein-Dracula Variation" in his 1976 book about Vienna Opening.\nThe position is, indeed, very delicate: White has a Rook more, but he is likely to lose the Knight in a8, so that he has actually only an exchange advantage. The backdraw of this material gain is the underdevelopment: during the first ten moves, White has touched four times his Queen's Knight that is about to be captured, and three times the Queen, so that his only developed light piece is the Bb3. Moreover, his Queen is in a risky position in the middle of the board, with very few escape routes in case she was attacked. On the contrary, Black has gained space with pawns, his Knights are active and the Bishops are ready to be placed on important diagonals. Black can therefore begin a dangerous attack.\nWhite must therefore consolidate his position. In parallel, he should prepare a counterattack against the opposite King, which is not well fortified. In the immediate, after a series of nearly forced moves, he has however various choices: he can try to recover his delay in development by playing moves such as d3, d4 or Nf3, bring the Queen to a safer place with Qf3, or even grab another pawn with Nxb6. According to the chess writer Carsten Hansen (as of 2000), this last choice is the main line. The move 11. d3 is instead described by Hansen as a previous main line, while Harding in 1998 considered it the most usual choice.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 e6 Bg5 dxc4 e4 b5 e5 h6 Bh4 g5 Nxg5 hxg5 Bxg5 Nbd7 g3
column3:
White prepares to fianchetto the light-squared bishop.
Blacks main response is 11...Bb7, fighting for the a8-h1 diagonal.
11...Rg8 is a sideline, preparing to exchange the rook for White's powerful dark-squared bishop. White ends up having a rook, a pawn and open lines on the kingside for the two pieces.
This move made its debut in 1944, in a game between Andre Lilienthal (whom the opening is named after) and Mikhail Botvinnik.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 Nbd7 Nxc4 Qc7 g3 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Bf4 Nfd7 Bg2
column3:
White develops the light-squared bishop and prepares to castle short.
From this position, two moves have been played historically: f6 and g5.
11...f6 is the old mainline, defending the knight.
11...g5 is the most popular line nowadays and is considered the best move for Black.

column1: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 O-O Qd2 Nc6 Bc4 Bd7 O-O-O Rc8 Bb3
column3: White correctly moves their bishop out of the c8 rook's line of fire with Bb3, keeping watch over Black's kingside. Now pawn attacks begin on  both sides, and speed and tempi are very important in these such attacks.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7 h5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 Bd2
column3: Still the main line. White prepares for queenside castling. Since we have played h2-h4-h5 before, it makes sense to launch a pawn storm on the kingside.\nBlack should continue with his development with moves like 11...Ngf6 or 11...Be7. After that, kingside castling is the only option. This leads to an intense battle later, while both side try to push their pawns to the enemy king's territory.\nTo avoid this, Black can try to castle on queenside with 11...Qc7 to control the b8-h2 diagonal, follow with 12...O-O-O.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5
column3: Black's knight must be saved from the combined attack by White's bishop and rook.\nWhen the American master Frank Marshall surprised future World Champion Jose Capablanca with the Marshall Gambit in 1918, his chosen follow-up was 11...Nf6, returning the knight to the kingside where Black's attack will be taking place.\nBut in the century since then, trial and error has caused 11...c6 to evolve into the main line.

column1: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 Nbd7 Nxc4 Qc7 g3 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Bf4 Nfd7 Bg2 g5
column3:
11...g5 is the most popular line nowadays and is considered the best move for Black. Because the kingside pawn structure is significantly weakened, Black will usually resort to castling queenside.
12. Bxg5?? would blunder 12...Nxc4. The bishop can't stay on the same diagonal as the black queen, so some pieces have to be traded.
12. Bxe5 allows Black to secure the bishop pair after 12...Nxe5 but White gets compensation after 13. Qd4 f6 14. O-O-O preventing Black from castling queenside.
12. Ne3 is played most often, planning to take the light-squared bishop. After 12...gxf4 13. Nxf5 O-O-O 14. Qc2 Black has two isolated pawns on the kingside, but a four on two majority on the queenside and has control of the d-file. White should soon castle short.
The Morozevich is named after the player Alexander Morozevich, who was the first person to play the variation and did so against Garry Kasparov in the year 2000.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7 h5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 Bd2 Ngf6
column3: A flexible move, since there are chances for Black to castle on both sides. Most of the time, White will play 12. O-O-O.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 c6
column3:
Black's move ...c6 nails down the d5-knight. For White to chop it off (12. Bxd5) would now leave Black with the bishop pair on an open board, and three queenside pawns that would tightly restrain White's four.
12. d4 is a natural developing move and the main line. Skip ahead to the first major fork in the road, which occurs after
12...Bd6 13. Re1 Qh4 14. g3 Qh3
12. d3 is a significant sideline favoured by Alexey Shirov. The pawn itself will be weaker for being on d3 instead of d4, but in return White gains the possibility of quickly converting the extra pawn into a passed pawn with a later c4 push. 12. d3 scores slightly better than 12. d4 at master level and is significantly less analysed.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7 h5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 Bd2 Ngf6 O-O-O
column3: Black is able to castle in the next two moves, either with 12...Bd6 13...O-O (12...Be7 is the same, since White will play 13. Ne2 anyway), or 12...Qc7 13...O-O-O.\nThe main line involves kingside castling.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 c6 d4
column3: 12...Bd6 is the universal response to 12. d4. Black's e7-bishop is hitting thin air on g5 and h4, so it relocates with gain of tempo to hit the much more exciting h2 square.

column1: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7 h5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 Bd2 Ngf6 O-O-O Be7
column3: Black prepares to castle on kingside with 13...O-O. White's most popular move is the prophylactic 13.Kb1, while other options include 13.Ne4 and 13.Qe2, continuing operations in the centre.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 c6 d4 Bd6
column3:
White has to move the rook from e5. The safest square for it is back on e1:
13. Re1
There's also the sideline
13. Re2
which seems to be motivated as much by novelty as anything else - the defence of f2 isn't generally an important factor, and the rook on e2 cuts the White queen's contact with h5 which gives Black the option of retreating her own queen there (from h3, after ...Qh4 g3 Qh3) in some lines.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 c6 d4 Bd6 Re1
column3: Black gets another free attacking move in this position, namely 13...Qh4 doubling the attack on the h2-pawn.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 c6 d4 Bd6 Re1 Qh4
column3: White has to do something about the double attack on h2. 14.h3 Bxh3! is a disaster, so it has to be 14. g3, one of the key moves of the Marshall Gambit proper.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 c6 d4 Bd6 Re1 Qh4 g3
column3: 14. Qh3 is the only move to save the queen while preserving some threats against the vulnerable White kingside.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 c6 d4 Bd6 Re1 Qh4 g3 Qh3
column3:
We've arrived at a critical point in the Marshall Gambit. Black has a simple threat of ...Bg4, after which the White queen will have to guard against the checkmate threat with ...Bf3 and ...Qg2. This would draw the queen away from the defence of the e1-rook, and the unsupported rook would then have difficulty resisting a Black takeover of the e-file starting with ...Rae8.
The old main line is 15. Be3. White pre-emptively blocks the e-file against Black's potential takeover. 15. Be3 makes sense in the context of White's development; the b1-knight will have to come to d2 if it hopes to influence matters on the kingside, but playing it immediately would box the c1-bishop in, so get that bishop out of the way first.
But what does the bishop do on e3? Well, nothing. Black has no threats against either f2 or d4, and a few moves down the line White may well be forced to meet a Black pawn push to f5 with the blocking move f4 (to stop Black playing ...f4 herself), at which point the bishop itself will be a target of the d5-knight and a rook on e8.
If White wants to take decisive action against the invading Black queen, the move 15. Re4 threatening Rh4 and preventing ...Bg4 is an excellent alternative to the main line. How excellent? Excellent to the tune of giving White 34% wins instead of 26%, and restricting Black to 23% wins instead of 32% (yes, Black wins considerably more games than White in the 15. Be3 line!) There is a caveat: White players of 15. Re4 are about 50 points higher rated to begin with. But there is a caveat to the caveat: after normalising for the White player's grade, 15. Re4 still outperforms 15. Be3 by about 80 points. In fact, as of 2018 White's last 13 wins against GM opposition have come in lines other than 15. Be3.

column1: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 c6 d4 Bd6 Re1 Qh4 g3 Qh3 Be3
column3: White has consolidated extra material/defenses on the kingside, while Black has a dangerous initiative targeting White's king with pieces like the queen on h3 and bishop on d6
